⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • According to recent reports, the best AI humanizer for web content is the one that changes how a draft reads without changing what it says.
  • According to recent reports, to compare them on equal terms, we ran the same 103-word AI-written release note through each tool in November 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

It has been revealed that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

According to recent reports, the best AI humanizer for web content is the one that changes how a draft reads without changing what it says. If you need a specific tone, Humanize Max gives you four styles and three lengths in one run. If you already work in QuillBot or Grammarly, their humanizers fit the account you have. GPTinf, Humanize AI and Undetectable AI put an AI check next to the rewrite, and Ahrefs gives you quick variants of a short passage.

According to recent reports, to compare them on equal terms, we ran the same 103-word AI-written release note through each tool in November 2026. It contains a product name, two image formats, a settings path and the word "must", so it shows whether a tool keeps the details a reader acts on. We also checked every feature, limit and price on the vendor's own pages on the same day.

A humanizer earns its place only if its output needs fewer fixes than the draft you started with, and these six checks show whether a tool will do that for your content.

In a recent development, humanize Max is a single-purpose humanizer: you paste an AI draft, upload a file or load the built-in sample, choose a style and a length, and get a rewritten version in a few seconds. The four styles are Academic, Casual, Creative and Formal, and the three lengths are Shorten, Standard and Expand, so you can turn a stiff feature description into casual blog copy and trim it in the same run.

The result highlights every phrase it changed, which makes it quick to check whether a product name or a settings path came through. If the rewrite doesn't land, Run it again produces a different version of the whole text. At the time of writing, it takes up to 2,000 words per run and works without an account.

Pricing: Plans and limits are still being finalized, so check the site for current terms.

Best for: Rewriting AI drafts of blog posts, product pages and emails into a specific tone.

It has been revealed that quillBot's AI Humanizer sits next to its paraphraser, grammar checker and AI detector, which makes it a natural pick if you already use QuillBot for rewording. Basic mode is free for up to 125 words per run, while Advanced mode, which rewrites more deeply, comes with Premium (the pricing page also lists three Advanced uses on the free plan). In our test, it asked us to create a free account before it showed the first result.

Premium removes the word limit and adds Freeze words, which keeps the terms you choose unchanged, along with tone insights, a history of past runs and a Chrome extension that humanizes text inside ChatGPT and Gemini.

Industry observers note that pricing: Basic mode is free. Premium is listed at $8.33 a month, billed annually.

Best for: Quick fixes to a paragraph or two for writers who already use QuillBot.

GPTinf is a writing toolkit built around its humanizer, with an AI detector, plagiarism checker, grammar checker, paraphraser and readability checker on the same site. The humanizer has two modes, Standard and Academic, and takes pasted text or a PDF, Word or plain-text file. File-to-File mode returns the humanized document in its original format, so a long brief keeps its layout.

It has been revealed that custom Style lets you paste 150 to 1,200 words of your own writing, and later runs are shaped to match it, with no account needed. After each run, an AI-likelihood estimate appears under the output, so you can see whether a draft needs another pass. Treat that number as a probability, not proof of who wrote the text.

It has been revealed that pricing: A free plan is available. Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for Lite (5,000 words), with Pro at $24.99 and Unlimited at $59.99.

Best for: Freelancers and content teams that want to rewrite and check drafts without switching tools.

Industry observers note that grammarly's AI Humanizer comes in two layers. The tool on its web page is free, works without an account and offers basic humanization of pasted text or an uploaded document. A free Grammarly account adds the Humanizer agent, with four preset styles, a custom voice built from a writing sample, and support for English, Spanish, French, German, Portuguese and Italian.

Grammarly says the humanizer focuses on clarity and readability rather than on AI detectors, which matches how most web teams use these tools. If you need to show how a piece was written, Grammarly Authorship reveals which parts came from AI, which came from online sources and which you wrote yourself. The basic tool's word counter allows up to 1,500 words per run.

Recent findings suggest that pricing: The basic humanizer is free. Grammarly Pro is listed at $12 on the prepares page, which doesn't state the billing period.

Best for: Teams that already write in Grammarly and want one voice across documents.

Humanize AI is built for people who want to tune the output. Without an account you get the Free tone, a Rewrite level slider with three stops (Quality, Balanced and Max) and Custom style, which learns your voice from 150 to 1,200 words of samples. A free account opens eight more modes, including Formal, Informal, Academic, Expand and Shorten, and on desktop a Writing level menu sets how plain or dense the result reads.

View changes highlights every edit, and File-to-File accepts PDF, DOCX, TXT and MD documents and returns them in the same format. Paid looks also include a public API that supports the same styles and rewrite levels as the web app, so a developer can add a humanizing step to a CMS or publishing pipeline.

Pricing: Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for Lite (10,000 words), with Standard at $19.99 and Unlimited at $59.99. Yearly billing lowers the monthly price.

Best for: Teams that need precise tone control or want to humanize text through an API.

Sources indicate that undetectable AI keeps its humanizer simple: one text box, one button and no style or length settings. Its free allowance works differently from the others, with 1,000 words in total before you need an account and another 1,000 once you create a free one.

Under the output, a Check for AI button runs a detection check on the result, and the same site has a separate AI detector and plagiarism checker. Its FAQ claims pasted text isn't published or shared but doesn't say whether it's stored, so keep confidential details out of the drafts you run through it.

Pricing: Paid intends start at $9.99 a month for Lite (5,000 words), with Pro at $25 (25,000 words) and Unlimited at $59 (1,000,000 words). Yearly billing lowers the monthly price.

Best for: Trying a humanizer on a full-length draft before you commit to an account.

Ahrefs, best known for its SEO platform, offers a free AI Text Humanizer among its writing tools. You paste up to 2,048 characters, choose one, three or five variants, and pick the version that reads best. It ran without an account in our test.

According to recent reports, variants are the useful part. For a hero headline, a meta description or a product blurb, comparing three rewrites side by side is faster than prompting a chatbot three times, and you can export all results as a text file. The character limit, which fits a few short paragraphs, rules it out for full articles.

Pricing: Free on Ahrefs' website.

Best for: Short marketing copy where you want several options to choose from.

The best AI humanizer tool for a documentation team isn't the one a growth marketer needs, so match the tool to the content in front of you.

It has been revealed that there isn't one winner, because these tools solve different problems. The quickest way to decide is to run a paragraph from your own work, ideally one with a product name, a number and an instruction, through two or three of the tools above, and keep the one whose output you'd publish with the fewest fixes.

Google's guidance on using generative AI content is about value rather than the tool: mass-producing pages that add nothing for readers can count as scaled content abuse. A humanizer changes phrasing, not usefulness, so the same rules apply. Google also recommends fact-checking AI-generated titles, meta descriptions and image alt text before you publish.

The best humanizer for your team is the one whose controls match your content: tone presets for blog posts, variants for short copy, change highlighting for docs and a custom voice for marketing. Run one of your own paragraphs through two or three tools from this list, then read every highlighted change, especially names, numbers and words like "must", before anything goes live.

#34765. Industry News: How the Supreme Court’s college admissions decision has changed the job pipeline for Black and Latino students

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 21m • 📚 Deep Dive (4157 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: How the Supreme Court’s college admissions decision has changed the job pipeline for Black and Latino students

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4157 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, jamila Chambers remembers when recruiters came to interview students at Occidental College with a clear mission: They wanted a diverse workforce.
  • Jamila Chambers remembers when recruiters came to interview students at Occidental College with a clear mission: They wanted a diverse workforce.
  • In a recent development, they interviewed juniors for internships that often led to full-time offers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, jamila Chambers remembers when recruiters came to interview students at Occidental College with a clear mission: They wanted a diverse workforce. They interviewed juniors for internships that often led to full-time offers. Finance firms came and ran affinity information sessions and job shadowing programs for first- and second-year students. “They would specifically say: ‘We’re looking for BIPOC students. We’re looking for first-gen students. We’re looking for LGBTQIA+ students,’” mentioned Chambers, executive director of the school’s Hameetman Career Center. Not anymore. Those pipelines, Chambers said, have “dried up.”  After a divided Supreme Court gutted race-conscious admissions in 2023, colleges could no longer give an edge to Black and Latino applicants over white and Asian applicants in the name of diversity, ushering in a new era for higher education. That meant the end of policies aimed at turning around historically low representation and systemic discrimination. The court’s ruling—which more than two-thirds of American adults told Gallup was “mostly a good thing”—did not address or change hiring laws nor mention employer efforts to make workplaces more inclusive. Yet many employers have since dismantled existing efforts to recruit diverse workers on college campuses, reporting by The Hechinger Report and Soledad O’Brien Productions found. Tech giant leaders removed or revised diversity language, changed recruitment strategies and reconsidered how they built pools of candidates, according to a Columbia Business School study based on a survey of human resources professionals. Half of those surveyed who were familiar with the ruling mistakenly believed it applied to workplaces; others feared becoming a target of lawsuits, public criticism, or political attention. They’re facing a hostile atmosphere. In January 2025, as one of the first acts of his second term, President Donald Trump issued an executive order that attacked so-called diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) hiring programs across federal agencies and contractors. Calling these efforts “discriminatory and illegal,” the order also pressured private employers to follow suit—including publicly traded corporations, large nonprofits, and universities with major endowments. Fear of drawing Trump’s ire appears to be the major reason many private employers have removed racial and gender representation goals from their hiring pipelines. Conservative legal activists used the Supreme Court ruling on affirmative action at colleges as a road map for targeting workplace programs that prioritize diversity. The Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank, urged businesses to remove or revoke corporate DEI positions, warning state and federal governments not to contract with corporations that have such statements. The full impact the ban on affirmative action at colleges will have on job placement won’t be known until 2028, once the first class of college students admitted since the decision graduates and enters the workforce. But one of the starkest consequences of both the court ruling and the pressures of the second Trump administration is already clear, as colleges and workplaces alike retreated from promises to fight racism and injustice through bolstered diversity programs that they made after the 2020 murder of George Floyd by a Minneapolis police officer. “I feel like this is clearly a backlash to that moment,” said Natasha Warikoo, a sociology professor at Tufts University who has studied affirmative action, noting that previously, a focus on racial justice “felt like a moral imperative.” Bryan J. Cook, director of higher education policy in the Work, Education, and Labor Division at the Urban Institute, said what he sees so far in early workforce trends is concerning, although he added that the midterm election’s sweeping verdict on Trump “could have some impact.” With Democrats controlling the House and Senate, he said, “It will be interesting to see if Congress pushes back on the administration’s anti-DEI efforts, including some to the DOJ investigations into schools’ admissions practices.” More than three dozen major companies contacted for this story—among them Meta, Google, Walmart, Target and Goldman Sachs—declined to discuss their recruiting practices, a stark contrast to companies’ previously publicized efforts to diversify their workforces. In addition, dozens of colleges approached for interviews would not make their career staff available or did not respond. Several counselors agreed to talk only if neither they nor their schools were named, citing concern about drawing the attention of the Trump administration. Following the court’s decision, Black enrollment declined or remained flat at nearly all highly selective private and public colleges—the 85 that accept 25% or less of applicants—and the same was true of Hispanic enrollment at more than half of those institutions. For example, at Harvard University, one of the defendants in the Supreme Court case, the percentage of incoming students who are Black has fallen by nearly half since 2023. That year, they made up 18% of the first-year class, while in 2026, they’re just 9.3%. Meanwhile, the path to the most prestigious entry-level jobs is also narrowing to favor students from a smaller set of largely private elite colleges—places where the entering classes are becoming less diverse, said Matt Sigelman, president of The Burning Glass Institute, a labor research firm. Before the decision, when companies and recruiters had broader diversity goals, they were casting a wider net, Sigelman said. And though the court decision was about college admissions, employers “could see the writing on the wall and changed the way they were hiring.” They put together guidance they were getting from the Department of Labor along with changes in the political culture, said Sigelman, and “in many cases pulled back from their diversity goals.’’ Burning Glass looked at the careers of 300,000 college graduates who entered the workforce between 2023 and 2025 to understand who landed where, and specifically who got jobs at the most competitive companies. Over that period, the share of those hires coming from the most elite colleges rose by nearly a third, according to the firm’s research, which typically draws on large databases of online career profiles, such as those on LinkedIn, and job postings. The results suggest that landing a good first job increasingly depends on which college a student gets into, and Sigelman thinks first-generation and minority students will remain at a particular disadvantage if they aren’t already known to employers. “What started as a decision about who gets admitted to college ultimately plays out in who gets a shot at the best employment,” Sigelman said. Other research on recruiting points yields similar findings. While nearly 60% of 150 major employers identified diversity as a priority for determining where to send campus recruiters in 2022, that figure was down to 31% in 2025, according to a survey by Veris Insights, a recruiting research firm. Over the same period, the share of major companies recruiting exclusively from a short list of schools rose from 17% to 26%, the survey found. There are also early signs that internships—an key employment pipeline for college students—are becoming more difficult for minority students to obtain, according to the National Association of Colleges and Employers, which connects college career offices with the employers that recruit from them. The association tracks the makeup of corporate internship programs, one of the main pipelines that companies used to diversify their workforce. It found that from 2021 to 2024, white students made up 50% to 53% of those interns. In the cohort that ran from fall 2024 through summer 2025, spanning Trump’s return to office, that share rose to 59%, said Shawn VanDerziel, the association’s president and CEO. He added that the weak job market, artificial intelligence, and inflation make it difficult to interpret this trend. California had already banned race-based affirmative action in public university admissions in 1996, with lasting consequences for students’ education and economic prospects, studies found. Still, recruiters regularly visited California’s campuses seeking out students of color, first-generation students, and women in science and engineering. But now, at the University of California, Berkeley, Santina Pitcher, senior associate director of employer relations, said federal agencies “from the Peace Corps to the State Department” have told her they can no longer explicitly recruit for diversity. Recruiters “weren’t approaching us in the same way” at Pomona College after the court ruling, said Hazel Raja, associate dean and senior director of the career development office on the private campus in Claremont, California. “My assumption is that there was a little bit of everybody pulling back to begin with, and then reassessing ways that they could still diversify their workforce in ways that still allowed for them to stay above the law in light of the policy changes,” Raja said. At San Jose State University, where more than 40% of students are the first in their families to attend college, the career center renamed some programs soon after the federal government changed its guidance in response to Trump’s executive order. References to DEI disappeared. What was once called a diversity job fair has been renamed the October Fest job and internship fair, said Lisa Trikofski, assistant director of employment engagement at the campus career center.Students say they can feel a shift underway. At San Jose State last spring, students moved through a career fair with résumés and rehearsed handshakes, navigating booths for companies that were looking to recruit. Winnie Tuban, who is Filipino and first in her family to go to college, said she enrolled at the school because it sits at the center of the design world she wanted to enter in Silicon Valley, close to headquarters for several tech company giants. Apple, Google, Meta, Adobe and Zoom recruited San Jose State graduates over the years and hired scores of them. Tuban has since graduated and ultimately found a job at a small startup in San Francisco on her own, not through recruiters. She said she found the landscape discouraging. “I feel like regardless of where you stand politically, when you’re living as a person of color and you hear that they’re ‘going to war on DEI,’ it makes it feel like you’re not welcome in that space,” she said. Daniella Mensah, a psychology major, was 2 when her family immigrated from Ghana. Her father works in government and her mother is a hairdresser, and she worries that students like her—people of color looking for their first job—are increasingly being overlooked because of policy changes. “I think a lot of companies don’t feel the need to work hard to allow other people of different backgrounds into those positions,” Mensah said. “It feels like an afterthought,” she added. “I think that has definitely affected the population entering those roles.”  There are many who believe that giving preferences to students like Mensah for both college admissions and jobs based on their identity is just wrong, including Frederick Hess, director of education policy studies at the American Enterprise Institute, a conservative think tank in Washington, D.C. That idea, Hess said, “far too often seems to have been reduced to counting the number of people from a particular race or ethnic group.”  In his view, real diversity would also mean hiring people from different regions, social classes, religions, and political outlooks. “Businesses can’t pretend that selecting employees based on skin color is a good proxy for all of the rich differences that they say they want to attend to,” he said. Back at Occidental College, Chambers, who is Black and in her 50s, worries her students are entering a job market where the legal and policy protections she relied on early in her career are being stripped away.In her office, she keeps a picture of the civil rights activist Ruby Bridges, who was 6 when she integrated an all-white elementary school in New Orleans in 1960. Bridges did that “so I can work in higher ed,” Chambers said. Now, she is having conversations with her own children that echo the conversations her parents had with her, in a very different era. “It is a challenge,” she said. “But we’re up for it.” This story was produced by The Hechinger Report, a nonprofit, independent news organization focused on inequality and innovation in education. Liz Willen and Maxine Paul Emile contributed reporting to this story about the end of affirmative action. It’s the third in a series of articles accompanying a documentary produced by a partnership between The Hechinger Report and  Soledad O’Brien Productions, about the ongoing impact of the Supreme Court ruling. “I think a lot of companies don’t feel the need to work hard to allow other people of different backgrounds into those positions,” Mensah stated. “It feels like an afterthought,” she added. “I think that has definitely affected the population entering those roles.”.

There are many who believe that giving preferences to students like Mensah for both college admissions and jobs based on their identity is just wrong, including Frederick Hess, director of education policy studies at the American Enterprise Institute, a conservative think tank in Washington, D.C.

That idea, Hess stated, “far too often seems to have been reduced to counting the number of people from a particular race or ethnic group.”.

Industry observers note that in his view, real diversity would also mean hiring people from different regions, social classes, religions, and political outlooks. “Businesses can’t pretend that selecting employees based on skin color is a good proxy for all of the rich differences that they say they want to attend to,” he mentioned.

Back at Occidental College, Chambers, who is Black and in her 50s, worries her students are entering a job market where the legal and policy protections she relied on early in her career are being stripped away.In her office, she keeps a picture of the civil rights activist Ruby Bridges, who was 6 when she integrated an all-white elementary school in Newly introduced Orleans in 1960.

Bridges did that “so I can work in higher ed,” Chambers noted.

Now, she is having conversations with her own children that echo the conversations her parents had with her, in a very different era.

Sources indicate that “It is a challenge,” she said. “But we’re up for it.”.

The price of success nobody warns founders about: Who are you after you sell your company?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2187 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, we entrepreneurs spend decades learning how to build, scale, and exit successful businesses, and there are countless books, podcasts, courses, and articles dedicated to the pursuit of this goal.
  • We entrepreneurs spend decades learning how to build, scale, and exit successful businesses, and there are countless books, podcasts, courses, and articles dedicated to the pursuit of this goal.
  • Yet almost nobody teaches us how to live after the exit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we entrepreneurs spend decades learning how to build, scale, and exit successful businesses, and there are countless books, podcasts, courses, and articles dedicated to the pursuit of this goal. Yet almost nobody teaches us how to live after the exit. In 2008, I did what most entrepreneurs dream of doing. I exited the business I’d spent nearly two decades building, just before the global financial crisis. By almost any measure, it was a remarkable success. What I discovered, and what I want to share with my fellow entrepreneurs, is that no one tells you about the psychological consequences of success. We celebrate the exit as the ultimate achievement: the culmination of years of sacrifice, sleepless nights, and relentless determination. A liquidity event takes place and the founder collects the check and disappears into a life of freedom and fulfilment. That’s the narrative, anyway. But my experience was very different, because my identity was fully linked to my business and everything it represented. I didn’t recognize it then, but I’d confused what I did with who I was. Without the business, I wasn’t entirely sure who I was anymore, and almost overnight my identity disappeared. What I’ve come to find out is that this is much more common than you may think it is. The hidden cost of no exit plan I built my property advisory business, Ober-Haus, after arriving in Estonia in the early 1990s, and developed it into a company that operated across seven countries. For nearly 20 years, my life revolved around building, negotiating, financing, and solving problems. I loved it and became good at it. Then I sold the company. Suddenly, I had the financial freedom I’d only dreamed about and spent most of my adult life pursuing—but that was when things began to unravel. Years before building Ober-Haus, I’d confronted alcoholism, entered recovery, and rebuilt my life. Yet I hadn’t fully recognized how easily the compulsive drive that once fueled my drinking could find a more socially celebrated outlet: ambition and success. After my exit, I moved to Argentina and immersed myself in a world of horses, polo, travel, and an extraordinary lifestyle. From the outside, it looked like the perfect reward for decades of hard work. Parts of it were wonderful, but something fundamental was missing. I’d spent so long pursuing financial independence that I hadn’t seriously considered what I would do with it once I had it. The adrenaline of building a business had been replaced by the pleasures of spending the proceeds. What I mistook for freedom was, in some ways, another form of escape. And the purpose of life disappeared slowly until finally it was gone. Over time, my wealth diminished. My marriage collapsed. I made difficult financial decisions and watched much of what I’d accumulated disappear. The exit that was supposed to secure my future became the beginning of one of the most difficult periods of my life, and came with a hidden cost that I’d never considered. A darker side to success Looking back, I can see that the problem began long before I sold my company. Entrepreneurs develop qualities that help us succeed: drive, competitiveness, resilience, an appetite for risk, and an almost obsessive determination to achieve our goals. These characteristics can build extraordinary businesses, but they don’t necessarily build extraordinary lives. We become accustomed to controlling outcomes, solving problems and measuring progress. We approach relationships like negotiations and personal fulfilment like another business objective. When something isn’t working, our instinct is to push harder or cut our losses. Success demands sacrifice; we accept that almost without thinking, whether it’s another missed family dinner, another canceled holiday, or another year promising ourselves that life will slow down after the next transaction. But there comes a moment when success starts asking for something we’re no longer willing to give. Our health. Our integrity. Our relationships. Perhaps even our sense of self. And the question becomes whether we can keep going without betraying ourselves further. This is the dark side of success that is rarely discussed—the problem with getting everything we ever wanted. Not because entrepreneurs don’t experience it, but because admitting it feels dangerously close to admitting failure. The answer isn’t another achievement When my life began falling apart, my instinct was familiar: start another business. I’ve done just that with a property credit business in the U.K., which restored direction, confidence, and financial purpose. What’s different this time around, however, is that I’ve come to understand that rebuilding a business and rebuilding a life are two different things. One can be measured in revenues, assets and returns. The other requires questions that don’t fit neatly into a spreadsheet: Who am I without the title? What do I actually want? Which relationships have I neglected? What am I still trying to prove, and to whom? These are uncomfortable questions for people accustomed to having answers, which is how many entrepreneurs operate. Yet avoiding them simply postpones the reckoning. It’s been hard to face this, especially when you consider that we live in a culture obsessed with optimization. We’re encouraged to extend our peak, maximize performance, preserve our youth, and constantly reinvent ourselves. While there’s nothing inherently wrong with that, sometimes this optimization becomes a sophisticated way of avoiding harder questions about identity, relationships, integrity and purpose. A changed relationship with success I want to share my story because I suspect there are thousands of successful founders wrestling with the question of who they are after the exit. From the outside, they appear to have everything. Inside, they’re wondering what happened. Today, in my sixties, I’m still an entrepreneur, still ambitious, and still interested in creating things. But the fundamental difference this time around is that my relationship with success has changed. I’m beginning to understand that my next chapter isn’t necessarily about becoming the version of the person I used to be—it’s about letting go of the person I no longer need to be. Contrary to what all the books and courses and stories tell you, the hardest part of success isn’t reaching the top. It’s actually when you discover that the person you became to get there is no longer the person you want to be. So if you’re an entrepreneur in a similar position, I invite you to consider the idea that your identity is more than your business achievements, and to then find the courage to build a life that doesn’t require you to keep climbing.

This new scorecard shows whether your favorite retailer is using Flock cameras

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1048 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Automated license plate readers from Flock Safety and other vendors have become increasingly controversial across the country after reports of misuse by officers, high error rates that can lead to dangerous police encounters, and concerns about access by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
  • Automated license plate readers from Flock Safety and other vendors have become increasingly controversial across the country after reports of misuse by officers, high error rates that can lead to dangerous police encounters, and concerns about access by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
  • Sources indicate that flock, in particular, operates a nationwide camera network, with data from cameras operated in one jurisdiction frequently accessed by investigators from elsewhere, making it hard for local officials to understand and control privacy risks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Automated license plate readers from Flock Safety and other vendors have become increasingly controversial across the country after reports of misuse by officers, high error rates that can lead to dangerous police encounters, and concerns about access by Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Flock, in particular, operates a nationwide camera network, with data from cameras operated in one jurisdiction frequently accessed by investigators from elsewhere, making it hard for local officials to understand and control privacy risks. As a result, while Flock and other providers emphasize that their cameras have been used to investigate legitimate crimes, rescue kidnapped kids, and track stolen cars, many municipalities have ended their contracts, in some cases even covering cameras awaiting removal by the service provider. Many businesses deploy their own automated license plate readers, or ALPRs, to track vehicles in their parking lots, sometimes sharing that information with law enforcement. But since private companies aren’t subject to freedom of information laws, it can be hard to know which businesses have them and what they’re doing with the data they collect. To help people understand in time for the holiday shopping season which stores use the devices, Fight for the Future just released a scorecard listing 10 major retailers and what the organization knows about their use of the cameras. “Retailers also need to be brought into the conversation,” says Reem Suleiman, senior campaign director at Fight for the Future, which previously organized a campaign with home improvement influencers that called on Home Depot and Lowe’s to cut ties with Flock. The chart is based on information the organization received from a questionnaire sent to the retailers and, in cases where they didn’t respond, third-party news reporting, crowdsourced camera spotting, and information from published privacy policies. “We got responses from just a handful of [businesses],” Suleiman says. The exact details vary, and many businesses don’t appear to use the technology at every location. Costco, for instance, told Fight for the Future that it uses ALPR cameras at “less than a dozen locations nationwide,” so it’s difficult to know just from the checklist whether your local branch of a national chain is equipped with the cameras. But it’s easy to see at a glance that many major brands at least acknowledge in their privacy policies that they might be using the technology. Some stores also indicate that they may share information from the devices with law enforcement. The scorecard offers links to retailers’ emails, along with suggested text, to ask them to refrain from using ALPR technology, even if (or perhaps especially if) the details about how they do so may be opaque. Fight for the Future also encourages people to reach out with any tips about retailers that are using the cameras or with requests to add particular stores to the scoresheet. “We don’t have a FOIA request that we can do for companies or a public records act request that we can impose upon companies, but nothing’s stopping us from writing to them,” Suleiman says. “Nothing’s stopping people from letting these companies know what they want and what they expect.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As consumers ready for the holiday season, it looks like gift shopping is taking a step away from the keyboard and moving back to brick-and-mortar locations. According to research from Alchemer’s 2026 Holiday Shopper Report, more U.S. shoppers are planning to shop in physical retail stores. Some 35.8% say they will mainly shop in person, versus 31% who initiative to shop mainly online. But surprisingly, the revival of in-store shopping is being driven by a generation that mostly missed out on the mall’s heyday: Gen Z. Research from the market research company Emarketer highlights that around 51% of Gen Z are opting to shop in stores rather than online or on apps. Their preferences are showing up in spending, too. Shoppers aged 18 to 24 made 62% of their purchases in physical stores last year, compared with 52% of those 25 and older. For Gen Z, a trip to a physical store is about more than just shopping. It’s an experience, and 63% of them say they bought something while there. The in-person shopping experience also has a social element to it. Nearly three in five Gen Z respondents say they shop as a way to spend time with others. The clothing aisle is leading the way back to the store, as around one in five Gen Zers say they visit a clothing store every month, twice the rate of all adults. Emarketer also found that many retailers are tapping into the renewed interest in real-world shopping, particularly catering to Gen Z. For instance, many are leaning on building community through in-store programming, like ornament making and letter-writing workshops at Macy’s, or fragrance readings at Lush, the personal care retailer. A unifying trend across ages is a low tolerance for friction. Customers are looking for smooth shopping experiences. Alchemer’s survey found that shoppers are particularly sensitive to disruptions like slow checkouts and items being out of stock.

The in-person shopping experience also has a social element to it. Nearly three in five Gen Z respondents say they shop as a way to spend time with others.

The clothing aisle is leading the way back to the store, as around one in five Gen Zers say they visit a clothing store every month, twice the rate of all adults.

Emarketer also found that many retailers are tapping into the renewed interest in real-world shopping, particularly catering to Gen Z. For instance, many are leaning on building community through in-store programming, like ornament making and letter-writing workshops at Macy’s, or fragrance readings at Lush, the personal care retailer.

According to recent reports, A unifying trend across ages is a low tolerance for friction. Customers are looking for smooth shopping experiences. Alchemer’s survey found that shoppers are particularly sensitive to disruptions like slow checkouts and items being out of stock.

Target’s Q3 2026 at a glance This morning before the opening bell, Target reported its Q3 2026 earnings, a period that ended on October 31. The company was facing challenges on multiple fronts. But Target was also facing a set of challenges unique to itself. Declining foot traffic had been driven by self-inflicted wounds over the years, including understaffed stores, messier merchandising, and DEI rollbacks that prompted a significant boycott of the company. When Fiddelke took the reins in February, he sought to correct many of these concerns, implementing sweeping changes, including a refined merchandising strategy that complemented Target’s strengths relative to competitors (such as well-designed home and apparel offerings). He also began remodeling stores to give them a new, modern look, and increased staffing at those stores to better meet customers’ needs. Those changes appear to be working. Target notes that in Q3, comparable foot traffic grew by 5%, while net sales grew 7.1% compared to last year. As CNBC noted, that’s Target’s best sales growth in more than five years. TGT shares have soared in 2026 A strong Q3 has led Target to update its expectations for fiscal year 2026. The company is now in its all-notable Q4, which covers the end-of-year holiday period. For fiscal 2026, Target says it now expects full-year net sales growth in a range of around 6%, which is one point higher than the 5% the company initially forecast. Still, despite the strong Q3 results, TGT shares are at the moment down about 1.1% in premarket trading, as of this writing. Some of that may be attributed to profit-taking. Target’s stock price has surged by more than 60% this year, and investors often decide to lock in profits after a good quarter. However, the drop in the company’s stock price may also signal investor concern about Target’s future business. There’s no doubt that Target was helped this quarter by its tariff refunds. That is an increase of $1 billion from what Target spent in 2026. While such spending may benefit Target in the long term, it can impact near-term growth, and investors generally think in the near term.

Retail giant Target Corporation (NYSE: TGT) has reported its third-quarter earnings for fiscal 2026, and they are a night-and-day difference compared to the results posted for the same quarter a year earlier.

Target’s sales growth for the period was the best in half a decade, suggesting that a turnaround proposal from its new CEO is working. Here’s what you need to know.

It has been revealed that this morning before the opening bell, Target reported its Q3 2026 earnings, a period that ended on October 31. By and large, the results were music to investors’ ears:.

Sources indicate that it should be noted that Target’s Q3 was helped somewhat by tariff refunds. During the quarter, the tech giant received $301 million back through refunds.

Those refunds contributed $228 million to net earnings as well as 50 cents to the company’s earnings per share for the quarter.

Even so, Target handily beat analyst expectations on several fronts, notes CNBC. Analysts had expected revenue of $26.5 billion and an EPS of $2.07. Even after discounting the 50 cent EPS tariff boost, Target would still have topped analysts’ expectations on earnings per share by 8 cents.

Announcing the results, Target’s CEO, Michael Fiddelke, who took the helm in February and immediately introduced a turnaround effort, noted the firm’s “third-quarter results reflect continued progress against our strategic priorities, centered on serving busy families with our signature blend of style, design and value.”.

A year ago, Target’s business looked much bleaker than it does today. The firm was facing challenges on multiple fronts.

Many retailers at that time were also facing some of those same challenges: increased tariffs and customers cutting back on discretionary spending as inflationary pressure bit into their pocketbooks.

But Target was also facing a set of challenges unique to itself. Declining foot traffic had been driven by self-inflicted wounds over the years, including understaffed stores, messier merchandising, and DEI rollbacks that prompted a significant boycott of the organization.

When Fiddelke took the reins in February, he sought to correct many of these issues, implementing sweeping changes, including a refined merchandising strategy that complemented Target’s strengths relative to competitors (such as well-designed home and apparel offerings).

He also began remodeling stores to give them a new, modern look, and increased staffing at those stores to better meet customers’ needs.

Industry observers note that those changes appear to be working. Target indicates that in Q3, comparable foot traffic grew by 5%, while net sales grew 7.1% compared to last year. As CNBC noted, that’s Target’s best sales growth in more than five years.

A strong Q3 has led Target to update its expectations for fiscal year 2026.

Sources indicate that the company is now in its all-notable Q4, which covers the end-of-year holiday period. For fiscal 2026, Target indicates it now expects full-year net sales growth in a range of around 6%, which is one point higher than the 5% the company initially forecast.

Still, despite the strong Q3 results, TGT shares are right now down about 1.1% in premarket trading, as of this writing.

Recent findings suggest that some of that may be attributed to profit-taking. Target’s stock price has surged by more than 60% this year, and investors often decide to lock in profits after a good quarter.

It has been revealed that however, the drop in the company’s stock price may also signal investor concern about Target’s future business. There’s no doubt that Target was helped this quarter by its tariff refunds. But those refunds won’t keep coming forever.

Additionally, Target remarked it expects its capex to be between $5 billion and $6 billion in 2027. That is an increase of $1 billion from what Target spent in 2026.

While such spending may benefit Target in the long term, it can impact near-term growth, and investors generally think in the near term.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, sankaet Pathak, founder and CEO of Foundation, tells Fast Manufacturer his company would consider arming its machines if asked to by the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Foundation Future Industries, a startup backed by Eric Trump, has unveiled a humanoid robot that can carry 200 pounds while walking through rain, snow, and dust. The organization wants its upcoming Phantom MKII to work on construction sites and in factories—but the CEO isn’t ruling out putting weapons in its hands. Sankaet Pathak, founder and CEO of Foundation, tells Fast Company his company would consider arming its machines if asked to by the U.S. military, arguing that deploying robots on the ground could reduce reliance on drones and air strikes. “We’re not anti-weaponization and warfare,” he states. “That’s not something we have a blanket policy of just saying we’re not going to do.” Phantom MKII is a second-generation humanoid designed for heavy industry and defense, unveiled today alongside Cortex II, the AI system that controls it. Foundation, which counts Eric Trump among its investors and advisers, has been particularly open about military applications—at times drawing controversy. Earlier this month, the Financial Times reported that Foundation’s cofounder and president, Mike LeBlanc, was in direct talks with the Israel Defense Forces to supply up to 1,000 of its first-generation Phantom MKI robots for operations in tunnels beneath Gaza. Pathak disputes that characterization. “We’re not in talks with the IDF in any official capacity on deploying robots there,” he says. “What we have are very early exploration conversations.” When pressed about LeBlanc’s comments, Pathak says there is “literally nothing actively going on,” and there are no conversations progressing toward a contract. Previously, Foundation remarked its machines had been tested with Ukrainian forces, while LeBlanc has described potential uses for them in detecting booby traps and trip wires. For now, Pathak says most of Foundation’s defense work focuses on logistics rather than combat—though he doesn’t rule out deploying his machines on the battlefield. “Any time DOW [Department of War] will come to us and say, ‘Well, we need these robots more on the active battlefield with a weapon,’ to me that indicates that means less drones, less air strikes, more precision,” he says. Pathak believes ground-based robots could accomplish military objectives without bombing entire buildings, potentially shortening wars. Whether deployed in war or on construction sites, which Pathak sees as the robot’s ideal initial use, the Phantom MKII is designed to be more capable than its predecessor. Foundation says the robot has weather-resistant joints and modular parts that can be replaced in the field, along with a battery that can run for up to six hours, though heavier payloads reduce that figure. At maximum capacity, Pathak says the machine can walk while carrying 200 pounds, compared with roughly 50 to 60 pounds for the previous version. The Phantom MKII can do so thanks to significant redesigns of its actuators, the motors and gearing that make its limbs move. Its joints have been shrunk to around three-quarters the size of its predecessor’s, Pathak says, while delivering more than 1.5 times the performance. Smaller also means somewhat cheaper. Pathak claims the company has halved its bill of materials cost while simplifying assembly to make large-scale manufacturing more practical. The goal is to begin producing MKII robots in early 2027. Initially, the company hopes to manufacture several hundred before ramping up to a few thousand by the end of the year. Production will initially remain in the San Francisco Bay Area; Pathak claims most components now come from the U.S. or allied countries. Alongside the hardware improvements, Foundation claims a significant leap forward in the software powering the machine. Its Cortex II artificial intelligence system is designed to learn physical tasks by observing humans perform them—requiring as few as 60 demonstrations for some tasks. Pathak’s ambitions extend beyond construction sites and battlefields, though he rules out selling to countries that aren’t allied with the United States. In a manifesto published alongside the robot’s launch, Pathak outlines a vision of the future in which fleets of robots work in mining, materials processing, and construction. Humanoids could help bring the cost of a $1 million home down to between $60,000 and $80,000, he figures. Beyond building your next home, the Phantom MKII could help keep it safe, too. Pathak is open to his robots taking on policing roles, provided they are deployed in ways that make people feel protected rather than intimidated. “I don’t think you can build a utopia and then not defend it,” he says.

#34752. From User Feedback to a Better Prompt: 4 Tools Tested in TypeScript

📅 08 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1780 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sitepoint ↗ Open Full Page

From User Feedback to a Better Prompt: 4 Tools Tested in TypeScript

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1780 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • According to recent reports, weekly.
  • When an LLM app gives a wrong answer, nothing in your logs reveals it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

According to recent reports, weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

When an LLM app gives a wrong answer, nothing in your logs reveals it. The request returns 200, the JSON is valid, and no exception fires. Usually the user is the only one who notices. A thumbs-down button records that moment, on the exact trace that went wrong, while the user still remembers why.

That button is easy to add. The hard part is what comes after: turning the thumbs-down into a reviewed test case, a judge score, and a better prompt.

In a recent development, we ran that loop in TypeScript in four tools: LangSmith, Langfuse, Phoenix and AcruxCore. All four handled the first four steps, which are user feedback, reviewer comments, a dataset and an LLM judge. Only AcruxCore rewrote the prompt from TypeScript. On 15 support tickets that no tool had seen, the rewritten prompt routed 13 correctly, against 7 for the original.

Recent findings suggest that our test app is a support-ticket router. It reads a ticket and returns JSON with a category (account, billing, bug or feature_request) and a priority (P0, P1 or P2). The first version of the prompt describes only the output format:.

Sources indicate that the support team has a policy that this prompt never states. Sign-in problems are always account. A customer who can't use the product at all is P0. Any billing error is P1, even when the customer claims there is no rush. Feature requests are P2, however angry the customer sounds.

Without that policy, the model guesses priority from the customer's tone. Here are three real replies from the first version:.

Every reply is valid JSON, so no schema check catches the mistake. A person has to read the reply and say it is wrong. The loop in this article takes that judgement and turns it into a better prompt.

In a recent development, all four tools cover evaluation. We compared the self-hosted ones on tracing in Self-Hosted LangSmith Alternatives: 4 Tools Tested on One TypeScript Agent, and on prompt registries in Prompt Management in TypeScript. For a broader comparison of self-hosted options, see this LangSmith alternatives roundup. This article covers the feedback loop only.

In a recent development, we wrote 30 tickets. Fifteen are the "production traffic" that each tool's app processed. The other 15 are a holdout set. No tool saw them, and we used them only for the final before-and-after check.

Each tool ran the same sequence from one TypeScript script:.

The reviewer comments follow one template, so the wording is identical in every tool:.

The comments name one rule each. The full policy appears nowhere in the data any tool received.

In a recent development, the app model isn't fully deterministic at temperature 0. Each tool's run got between 6 and 8 of the 15 traffic tickets right, so the tools received 7 to 9 thumbs-down each. The holdout check below repeats every measurement three times.

All four tools accept feedback on a trace from TypeScript. They differ in how a second person, the reviewer, adds the correct answer.

LangSmith stores both as feedback on a run. The thumbs-down runs go into an annotation queue, where a reviewer adds feedback with a comment:.

According to recent reports, langfuse stores both as scores. An annotation queue needs a score config first:.

Industry observers note that phoenix stores both as span annotations. The reviewer's comment goes in explanation:.

Industry observers note that phoenix stores spans asynchronously. Our first run annotated a span before Phoenix had stored it, and the API returned a 404. The script now waits until all 15 spans are visible.

AcruxCore stores both as feedback rows on the trace. The source field separates the end user from the reviewer:.

Industry observers note that this is the first step where the code differs a lot. Each tool can make a dataset, but only one builds it from feedback in one call.

Industry observers note that in LangSmith, a run query finds the thumbs-down runs. Then createExamples copies them into a dataset. You decide where the reviewer's comment goes. We put it in the reference output:.

According to recent reports, langSmith can also do this without code. An automation rule in the UI can add runs that match a filter to a dataset.

In a recent development, in Langfuse, the scores API finds the thumbs-down traces. Two details cost us a run each. A boolean score is filtered with value: "false", not 0. And the trace ID is returned only when you ask for the subject field group:.

In Phoenix, getSpans can't filter by annotation. So the script lists the app's spans, reads their annotations, and keeps the ones with a thumbs-down. Then createDataset takes the examples. We kept the source span ID in the metadata.

In AcruxCore, buildFromFeedback takes the reviewer's feedback IDs. Each comment becomes that example's grading criteria, and the input comes from the variables captured on the trace:.

Each tool scored the first version of the prompt on its own dataset. The judge read the reviewer's comment and the router's reply, and returned 1 for a match and 0 for a mismatch.

It has been revealed that langSmith, Langfuse and Phoenix each have an experiment runner that takes your evaluator function, and we gave all three the same judge prompt. AcruxCore grades with its built-in judge inside the optimize run. All four used the same judge model.

The first version fails almost every reviewed case. That is expected, because these are the cases owners marked wrong. A score of 1 means the app model got that case right on the second call, or the judge accepted a wrong reply. We didn't check which.

In a recent development, the judge can also run without your code. Besides the in-code evaluator we used, Langfuse has a managed LLM-as-a-judge that runs on production traces and on experiments, with your own judge prompt. LangSmith has online evaluators, which you set up in its UI, for the same job.

An optimizer reads the failing cases and the reviewer comments, writes new versions of the prompt, and scores each one with the judge. This is the step that turns feedback into a better prompt, and it's where the four tools differ most.

LangSmith's API reference lists an optimize prompt job (POST /api/v1/repos/optimize-job). It takes a prompt name, a dataset name, evaluator IDs and an algorithm, promptim or demo. No method in the TypeScript SDK wraps it, so we called it with fetch. We gave it a code evaluator that checks the reply against the reviewer's correct answer.

The job was accepted and reported successful about ten seconds later. It ran no experiment on the dataset. With auto_commit set to true, it added no fresh commit to the prompt. We found no guide for this endpoint, so we may have configured it wrongly, but the job record and its logs gave no error to act on.

LangSmith's documented route to prompt optimization is promptim, which its README calls an experimental library. It is a Python package with a CLI, and it can add a human review step through LangSmith annotation queues.

Langfuse has no optimizer. Its blog highlights a workflow with Claude Code agent skills that reads Langfuse data and edits the prompt. That workflow runs in a coding agent, not in your app's code.

Phoenix's Optimize Prompts Automatically tutorial uses Arize's prompt-learning package, which you clone from GitHub and install with pip. The Phoenix TypeScript client has no optimizer export, and the tutorial runs outside Phoenix. Arize's commercial platform, Arize AX, has prompt optimization built in.

It has been revealed that for Python teams, there are more options: Opik's Agent Optimizer and DSPy both rewrite prompts from a dataset and a metric. This article covers TypeScript.

Sources indicate that its optimize run takes the dataset and drafts three rewrites of the production prompt. It runs each rewrite and the current production version on every example, and the judge grades all of them:.

The run finished with this report:.

The three rewrites tied, so we took candidate A. Its rationale: "Added explicit priority rules for each category and clarified that access-blocking challenges are P0, billing errors are P1, and feature requests are P2, overriding tone/urgency." The Improve a prompt from feedback guide covers the dashboard version of this step.

A rewrite that passes the cases it was built from can still fail on newly introduced tickets. So we ran both prompts on the 15 holdout tickets, three times each, outside every tool. The script calls the model directly and checks the category and the priority against the expected answer. No judge is involved.

The two misses are worth reading:.

In a recent development, both come from one line in the rewrite: "P1 for bugs without workaround." That rule isn't in the team's policy, and no reviewer wrote it. The optimizer made it up to explain the examples it had. There was also no outage in the traffic set's thumbs-down cases, because the first version routed that one correctly. So no comment ever said that a full outage is P0.

In a recent development, the optimizer learns only from what owners marked wrong. Anything they never marked stays a guess, and the rationale won't tell you which rules are guesses. Read the rewritten prompt before you promote it.

In LangSmith, Langfuse and Phoenix, shipping a new version is a tag or label move. We showed those calls in the prompt-management article. Here there was no rewrite to ship, so the step didn't apply.

According to recent reports, in AcruxCore, promotion commits the candidate as a upcoming prompt version and moves the production alias to it. Nothing else moves:.

The app renders production on every call, so the next ticket used version 2 without a deploy.

Recent findings suggest that use LangSmith if your team already works in it and writes Python. Feedback, queues, datasets and experiments all work from TypeScript, and promptim covers optimization from Python.

Use Langfuse if you want a managed judge that runs on live traces with your own prompt. Plan to write the dataset glue code and the rewrite step yourself.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, after a 13-year wait, one of entertainment’s biggest releases is finally here.“Grand Theft Auto VI” launches Thursday, sending players back to Vice City and testing whether Rockstar Games can follow one of the bestselling video games ever made with another cultural and commercial phenomenon.The latest installment becomes playable at midnight local time on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X’S, meaning players in Asia and other regions will begin entering the game hours before its U.S. release.New Zealand will be among the first countries where players can access the game and internet providers there are preparing for a surge in downloads as midnight arrives.“The game file size at 212 gigabytes is unprecedented,” remarked Kurt Rodgers, network strategy manager for Chorus New Zealand. “That’s more than a quarter of the average household’s data usage in an entire month, all in one go.”The company expects about 35 petabytes of additional traffic across its network, which Rodgers called “enormous.”The expectations are enormous, too.The “Grand Theft Auto” franchise has sold more than 470 million units worldwide, while “Grand Theft Auto V,” released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those sales and reached $1 billion in retail sales in just three days.Rockstar is returning to Vice City, its fictionalized version of Miami, with two new protagonists, a sprawling Florida-inspired world and the pressure of following a game that became one of the most successful entertainment products ever released. Game returns to Vice City after 13 years At the center of “GTA VI” are Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple whose attempts to improve their lives pull them deeper into the criminal underworld of Leonida, Rockstar’s fictionalized version of Florida.Lucia has recently been released from prison, while Jason is a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the Leonida Keys. When a criminal job goes wrong, the pair become entangled in a wider conspiracy.Their relationship marks one of the biggest departures from “Grand Theft Auto V,” which followed three playable protagonists.Rockstar has promoted Leonida as its largest and most detailed open world yet, stretching beyond Vice City into beaches, highways, wetlands, nightlife districts and smaller communities inspired by South Florida.Developers immersed themselves in the region while building the game, driving through Miami, the Florida Keys and surrounding communities. They flew over the Everglades and researched the area’s history and architecture. Miami embraces its fictional alter ego Miami and surrounding communities have leaned into their connection to Vice City ahead of the release, with businesses, sports teams and local governments using the game’s arrival as a marketing opportunity.Miami-Dade County entered into a $3.9 million promotional deal with Rockstar that includes a giant “Welcome to Vice City” display atop the Miami Heat’s Kaseya Center. The NBA team is also scheduled to wear black-and-pink Vice City uniforms on the eve of the game’s release.The campaign has not been universally welcomed. Some South Florida officials have questioned whether public resources should be used to promote a franchise known for car theft, gunplay and other criminal activity.Supporters have argued that the enormous attention surrounding “GTA VI” gives the region an opportunity to capitalize on a global spotlight.In Seoul, a giant advertisement draped the side of a building, while Warner Music will host a party at a bar Thursday themed around the game’s soundtrack. Years of hype arrive at launch day Few entertainment releases arrive with this much anticipation.The first “GTA VI” trailer drew more than 93 million YouTube views in its first 24 hours, while Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent company, has said the second trailer generated more than 475 million views across platforms in a day.The game also has attracted awards attention before most players have had a chance to explore it.“GTA VI” received eight nominations Tuesday for the Game Awards, including game of the year, game direction, narrative, art direction, score and music, audio design, action/adventure and performance. The awards will be presented Dec. 10.The long wait is partly a product of the extraordinary staying power of its predecessor. “Grand Theft Auto Online,” the multiplayer component of “GTA V,” has kept players engaged for years through updates, activities and in-game purchases.Music has long been woven into the “Grand Theft Auto” experience, with fictional radio stations and carefully curated soundtracks accompanying players as they drive through the series’ cities.For “GTA VI,” Rockstar commissioned an original adaptive score from Grammy-winning French electronic duo Justice. The music is designed to shift depending on where players are and what they are doing. A 30-track “Grand Theft Auto VI: Original Score” is scheduled for release Dec. 11 and includes collaborations involving Tame Impala, SZA, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard and Gesaffelstein. What players will find next Despite years of trailers and promotional material, Rockstar has kept significant portions of “GTA VI” under wraps.The full voice cast has not been revealed, including the performers behind Lucia and Jason. Actor Stephen Root has confirmed to The Associated Press that he appears in the game, though Rockstar has not publicly identified his role.Questions also remain about the full range of characters, locations, activities and gameplay systems waiting inside Leonida.Those answers will begin emerging first from players in Asia and Europe as midnight arrives in their regions, followed by North America hours later. Associated Press journalists Charlotte Graham-McLay and Tong-hyung Kim contributed to this report. —Jonathan Landrum Jr., AP Entertainment Writer.
