Friendly Fraud Prevention for Developers: What to Log, Block and Automate

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2573 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Sources indicate that friendly fraud prevention comes down to three jobs you can do in code: log the right checkout data, block risky payments before they settle, and automate your response when a dispute still lands.
  • Recent findings suggest that in this tutorial, we'll build each piece in Node.js in a way that works with any payment service provider (PSP).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

It has been revealed that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Sources indicate that friendly fraud prevention comes down to three jobs you can do in code: log the right checkout data, block risky payments before they settle, and automate your response when a dispute still lands. Get the first one wrong and you can't win the dispute later, no matter how good your case is.

Recent findings suggest that in this tutorial, we'll build each piece in Node.js in a way that works with any payment service provider (PSP). Your code owns the data and the logic, and a thin adapter talks to Stripe, Adyen, Checkout.com or whoever processes your payments.

Friendly fraud happens when a customer makes a real purchase, then disputes it with their card issuer. They might claim they didn't authorize it, that it never arrived, or that they canceled. Sometimes it's honest confusion. A spouse used the saved card, or the charge highlighted up under a name they didn't recognize. Sometimes it's a free refund with extra steps.

Either way, the money leaves your account. A dispute (also called a chargeback) reverses the payment, and your processor charges a dispute fee on top. Lose too many, and the card networks put your account into a monitoring program with higher fees.

Sources indicate that it's also common. Visa puts friendly fraud at around 20% of fraudulent disputes globally, and up to 30% for high-volume online merchants. Mastercard goes further: it says first-party fraud makes up 75% of the fraud online businesses experience.

So why is this your problem and not finance's? Because the evidence that wins these disputes is created at checkout, by your code. If your app never stored the customer's IP address, device ID or login history, nobody can produce it three months later when the dispute arrives.

Friendly fraud can be stopped at four points, and each one is a different piece of code:.

It has been revealed that most guides only cover stages 1 and 4. The rest of this tutorial walks through all four.

Industry observers note that log four things on every order: the customer's IP address, a device ID, their account ID and the shipping address. Those are the data elements Visa's Compelling Evidence 3.0 (CE3.0) rules check when you fight an "unauthorized" fraud dispute.

Industry observers note that here's how CE3.0 works. You win the dispute if you can show two earlier, undisputed purchases on the same card, made 120 to 365 days before the disputed one. All three purchases must share at least two data elements, and one of them must be the IP address or device ID. In plain terms: same card, same person, same device, and they never complained before.

Most PSPs support CE3.0, including Stripe, Adyen, Checkout.com and Airwallex. But none of them can submit data you never captured. And because the window reaches back a full year, you need to keep these logs for at least 13 months (Mastercard's rule, below).

According to recent reports, mastercard has its own version, called First-Party Trust, for disputes filed under reason code 4837 (no cardholder authorization). It asks for one data point from each of three categories: a device factor (IP address, device ID or fingerprint), a delivery factor (shipping address, email or phone) and a different identity factor (such as account login ID or billing address). On the dispute route, Mastercard calls a lookup service that you host, with named fields such as deviceIpAddress, orderDeviceId, orderEmail and userIdName. That service has to answer in about 2.5 seconds on average and search 13 months of sales data.

First-Party Trust is live in the US. Per Mastercard's October 2026 announcement, it reaches Eastern Europe, the Middle East and Africa from October 2026 and the rest of Europe from July 2027. If you sell into Europe, the logging work is due now.

Two storage rules save you pain later:.

Recent findings suggest that the good news: one evidence table serves both networks. Capture the data once, then keep the eligibility checks for Visa and Mastercard separate.

Start with a table that stores this data per order, separate from your PSP:.

Then capture it in your checkout route. If your app sits behind a proxy or CDN, set Express's trust proxy so req.ip returns the customer's address, not your load balancer's:.

It has been revealed that the psp object is your adapter: one small module per provider that maps its API to the same shape. Swap providers, and this route doesn't change.

According to recent reports, for digital products and SaaS, log usage too. Login timestamps, downloads and feature activity prove the customer used what they paid for, which beats "I never received it" claims.

Sources indicate that the cheapest dispute is the one that never happens. Three checkout changes do most of the work: 3D Secure on risky payments, a billing descriptor customers recognize, and a few rules that stop obvious abuse.

Use 3D Secure where risk is higher. 3D Secure (3DS) asks the cardholder to confirm the payment with their bank, often through an app prompt. For authenticated payments, liability for fraud disputes generally shifts from you to the card issuer. Every major PSP supports it, and most let you request it per payment instead of forcing it on everyone. Forcing it everywhere adds friction and costs conversions, so trigger it on risk signals.

Make your billing descriptor obvious. The descriptor is the text on the customer's card statement. If it reads PMT*SRV 8812 instead of your product name, expect "I don't recognize this charge" disputes. Use the brand name customers know, and add a support URL or phone number where your PSP allows it. If you sell several products, use a dynamic descriptor that names each one.

Add a risk check before you charge. Most PSPs include a rules engine, but a small check in your own code keeps the logic portable:.

Store the signals array with the order. If a dispute arrives later, you'll know whether the payment looked risky at the time, which helps you decide whether to fight it or accept it.

Keep the rules few and specific. A rule that blocks 5% of good customers to stop 1% of bad ones costs more than the disputes it prevents.

Yes, if you ship physical goods. The window between a successful payment and the moment an order ships is the cheapest place to stop friendly fraud: nothing has left the warehouse, so canceling costs you nothing but the sale. Most fraud tools decide at checkout and never look again.

The pattern is a fulfillment gate. Instead of sending every paid order straight to your warehouse or 3PL, route it through a decision step first:.

The verify path does two jobs. Legitimate buyers confirm and their order ships. Buyers planning to dispute see that the store is watching, and a confirmed verification becomes evidence if they dispute anyway.

The hard part is screenOrder. Your own data only demonstrates how a customer behaved with you. A buyer who has filed "item not received" disputes at 10 other stores looks brand new on their first order with yours. That's why post-purchase screening works best on shared data across many merchants.

In a recent development, chargeflow Prevent is one example of this kind of friendly fraud prevention. It scores each order after checkout and before fulfillment, links device, IP, email and payment behavior across a network of 20,000+ merchants, and returns approve, verify or cancel. Today it runs as a Shopify app, with no checkout changes. A public Prevent API isn't available yet, so on other stacks you'd build the gate above with your own rules and data.

Build an order lookup endpoint. When a cardholder taps "I don't recognize this" in their banking app, the issuer can now ask the merchant for order details before a dispute is filed. Visa does this through Verifi Order Insight, and Mastercard through Ethoca Consumer Clarity. Show the customer a receipt with your logo, the items and the delivery date, and many disputes are never filed.

It has been revealed that one endpoint can serve both networks, plus Mastercard's First-Party Trust dispute route. Mastercard's published service levels for this kind of lookup are strict:.

Sources indicate that the tricky part is matching. Issuers often send partial data, so match on whatever arrives: acquirer reference number (ARN), authorization code, date, amount, currency, and card BIN plus last four digits.

Industry observers note that on top of lookups, Visa and many PSPs offer rules-based auto-refunds. Verifi's Rapid Dispute Resolution (RDR) and Visa Resolve refund pre-disputes that match rules you set, such as "refund anything under $25". You don't write code for these, but you do pick the thresholds, so treat them like the REFUND_THRESHOLD below.

Sources indicate that if you sell subscriptions, many friendly fraud disputes aren't about stolen cards at all. The customer forgot about a renewal, couldn't find the cancel button, or thinks they canceled. Each of these has a code fix.

Here's a daily job that sends renewal reminders and records that each one went out:.

That evidenceLog row matters. When a customer later claims they never knew about the renewal, you can show the exact date you told them.

Automate two things: refunding payments that get flagged before they become chargebacks, and building evidence packets for the ones you fight. Both run off webhooks, and both have hard deadlines that humans miss.

Recent findings suggest that card networks can warn you before a dispute is filed. Visa runs this through Verifi and Mastercard through Ethoca, and many PSPs pass these alerts or their own early fraud warnings to you by webhook. Refunding at this stage costs you the sale, but you skip the dispute fee and the dispute doesn't count against your ratio.

The threshold is a business call. Refunding a $20 order is cheaper than fighting it; a $900 order with strong evidence may be worth contesting.

When a fraud dispute arrives, check whether it qualifies for CE3.0 by looking for two earlier undisputed orders on the same card that share data with the disputed one:.

If you get two matches, pass them to your PSP's CE3.0 evidence fields. On Stripe that's evidence.enhanced_evidence.visa_compelling_evidence_3; other PSPs have their own equivalents. Your adapter handles the mapping. If not, fall back to standard evidence: the IP, receipt, usage logs, renewal reminders and terms acceptance you've been logging all along.

Recent findings suggest that always submit before the deadline your PSP returns with the dispute. A late response is an automatic loss.

It has been revealed that the code above covers the basics. A production system also needs evidence templates per reason code, network deadlines per card brand, retries, and win-rate tracking. That maintenance multiplies with every PSP you add.

PSP-native tools only see that PSP's data, so they miss the usage logs, renewal reminders and support threads in your own app. A dedicated platform connects to your PSPs and lets you send that data in.

Here's what the buy path looks like with the Chargeflow API. Chargeflow ingests disputes from connected PSPs (Stripe, PayPal, Adyen, Checkout.com, Braintree and 20+ others), fires a dispute.created webhook, and you enrich the dispute with the evidence you logged:.

Chargeflow then builds the response and submits it to the PSP before the deadline. Pre-dispute alerts work the same way: Chargeflow can refund flagged transactions for you, or send alerts.created and alerts.transaction.linked webhooks so your code complications the refund and reports the result to POST /alerts/{id}/outcome.

Using Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor to build this? Chargeflow publishes its whole developer documentation as one machine-readable file, docs.chargeflow.io/llms-full.txt. Point your assistant at it and it can write the webhook handler and field mapping against the real API, not a guess.

Recent findings suggest that then your merchants get the disputes, and you need to give them a dispute product without building a dispute team. Chargeflow Connect is built for this. It exposes the same prevention, alerts and recovery engine to your platform in a few delivery models:.

According to recent reports, eaaS is the most developer-friendly entry point. You POST /public/2025-04-01/evidence with a merchant account_id and a dispute, get back an in_progress record, and receive an evidence.ready webhook with the PDF link, typically in about 30 seconds. Store the evidence id, not the URL, because the download link expires after 7 days. You can run it on auto-pilot (Chargeflow generates and submits) or co-pilot (your merchant approves first).

Sources indicate that don't wait for a customer to dispute a charge to find out your evidence pipeline is broken. Most PSPs give you test cards that create disputes on demand.

One more check before launch: confirm your webhook endpoints verify signatures and return 200 fast. PSPs and Chargeflow retry deliveries that fail, and a slow handler can process the same dispute twice.

According to recent reports, if you only do one thing this week, start logging IP address and device ID on every order. Everything else builds on that data.

True fraud is when a criminal uses a stolen card. Friendly fraud is when the real cardholder makes a purchase, then disputes it. Prevention differs: true fraud is stopped at checkout with risk checks and 3DS, while friendly fraud is won with evidence after the fact.

Mostly, yes. Both describe a real cardholder disputing a legitimate charge. "Chargeback fraud" usually implies the customer did it on purpose, while friendly fraud also covers honest mistakes, like a forgotten subscription or a family member's purchase. Visa calls it first-party misuse, and Mastercard calls it first-party fraud.

Check the reason code first. For "unauthorized" fraud claims, submit Visa CE3.0 or Mastercard First-Party Trust evidence if the customer qualifies. For "not received" or "canceled" claims, submit delivery proof, usage logs and your cancellation records. For low-value orders, accepting the dispute or refunding on an alert is often cheaper than fighting it.

Partly. 3DS generally shifts liability for fraud disputes to the issuer, so "I didn't authorize this" claims on authenticated payments rarely cost you. It doesn't help with "item not received" or "I canceled" disputes, which need delivery proof and cancellation records.

Sources indicate that no. CE3.0 needs two undisputed purchases on the same card made 120 to 365 days earlier, so it only protects returning customers. For first-time buyers, rely on 3DS and standard evidence.

Recent findings suggest that yes. Mastercard's First-Party Trust program covers reason code 4837 disputes. It needs one device, one delivery and one extra identity data point, and Mastercard checks them against the cardholder's past purchases. The same evidence table you build for Visa feeds both.

It has been revealed that it depends on the stage. At checkout, your PSP's 3D Secure and rules engine. After payment, post-purchase screening such as Chargeflow Prevent holds risky orders before they ship. Before a chargeback, Verifi Order Insight and Ethoca Consumer Clarity show cardholders the order details, while Verifi and Ethoca alerts (offered by many PSPs and by Chargeflow Alerts) and RDR let you refund early. After a chargeback, Visa CE3.0, Mastercard First-Party Trust and dispute automation tools submit the evidence. For developers, the Chargeflow API covers the alert and dispute stages across PSPs, and Chargeflow Connect does the same for platforms.

Arion Kurtaj leaked 90 videos of GTA VI years before its release.

Arion Kurtaj leaked 90 videos of GTA VI years before its release.

Arion Kurtaj, a member of the Lapsus$ cybercrime group who leaked 90 videos of Grand Theft Auto VI in 2022 and hacked other big companies, pleaded guilty on Monday, according to the UK’s Crown Prosecution Service (CPS).

Kurtaj, who is now 21, hacked BT/EE sometime between August and November 2021, and starting in early November of that year, the firm “noted a marked increase in unauthorised SIM swaps of their customers mobile phones.” He was charged for those offenses and moved to a hotel for his “own protection” in September 2022, but “breached his bail conditions to carry out further hacks on major companies using a mobile phone, the hotel TV’s Wi-Fi and a firestick,” including hacks on Rockstar Games, Uber, and Revolut, the CPS indicates.

He was sentenced to life in a secure hospital in December 2023 because of his autism, but in January, Kurtaj was deemed fit for trial and moved to prison, the BBC reports.

According to recent reports, kurtaj is set to be sentenced on November 23rd. GTA VI will be released on November 19th.

Recent findings suggest that the product carousel looks finished. The image fills the card, the price sits under the product name, and the arrow on the right takes you to the next item. The demo goes smoothly.

According to recent reports, then you put the mouse down. You press Tab, and focus skips the arrows entirely. If you rely on a keyboard, the first product is the only one you can reach.

Sources indicate that that’s a front-end bug hiding in plain sight. It’s also a good illustration of where AI fits into front-end development. A prompt can describe what a component should look like and what should happen on click. The implementation still has to account for how people reach that control, activate it, and understand what changed.

Imagine asking an AI coding assistant for this:.

Recent findings suggest that build a React product carousel with previous and next arrows. Show one product at a time and wrap around at the ends.

Here’s an illustrative excerpt from the sort of implementation that can satisfy a quick mouse-driven demo:.

Industry observers note that with some CSS, this can look exactly like the arrow in the design. The click handler advances the slide. A screenshot indicates the right layout.

But a plain div sits outside the normal Tab sequence and has no native button semantics or keyboard activation. Adding tabIndex={0} would make it reachable while leaving Enter and Space behavior to be implemented separately. The browser already provides those behaviors through a native button.

The real omission was in the requirement. “Show arrows” described the visual design. “Let someone reach and operate both controls with a keyboard” describes behavior you can test.

According to recent reports, here’s a small version of the same carousel. The product data is fixed for the example, and the slides change only when the user requests it.

It has been revealed that the buttons have visible labels and work with both Enter and Space. When a slide changes, focus stays on the button you pressed, so you can press it again to keep browsing. The status message gives assistive technology a way to announce the fresh product and its position. Only the current product link is rendered, so Tab never lands on a link from a hidden slide.

It has been revealed that those are deliberate interaction choices. W3C’s carousel pattern provides guidance on using native buttons, keeping focus on the slide controls after activation, and handling automatic rotation when a design requires it. W3C Carousel Pattern.

I’d revise the original prompt like this:.

Build a manual React product carousel. Use native Previous and Next buttons. Both must work with Tab, Enter, and Space. Keep focus on the activated button after a slide change. Announce the new product name and position through a status message. Keep only the current product link in the Tab sequence. Show what happens when the user advances past the last product.

The extra detail also gives you a review plan. For this carousel, I’d use four checks:.

Recent findings suggest that AI can help draft automated tests for the active link and wraparound behavior. I’d still run the keyboard and screen reader checks on the integrated page. A global stylesheet can erase a visible focus outline. A surrounding component can introduce an extra tab stop. The experience depends on the page the customer actually uses.

Industry observers note that A checkout form can look complete with sample data and lose the customer’s entries when a request fails. A responsive header can match the design at two widths and overlap when a translated label is longer. A component can render correctly in isolation and shift the page when a slow image loads.

According to recent reports, each example gives AI a concrete job. Ask it to preserve form values after a failed request, check the header with longer labels, or reserve space for the image. Then reproduce the condition yourself. Knowing which conditions matter is part of knowing the front end.

Recent findings suggest that the next time AI gives you a carousel that looks ready, start the review with your hands off the mouse. Tab to Next, press Space twice, and see where focus lands. That short test gives you evidence about how the component works for someone who relies on a keyboard.

#34719. Xreal Aura Review: Android XR combined with lightweight glasses delivers a true next-gen spatial computing experience

Xreal Aura Review: Android XR combined with lightweight glasses delivers a true next-gen spatial computing experience

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2282 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you can get past the $1,000+ price of entry, the Xreal Aura really ups the ante for low-impact spatial computing.
  • Powerful Computing Puck adds another form of input.
  • Familiar Android XR interface+ Access to the vast Android ecosystem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you can get past the $1,000+ price of entry, the Xreal Aura really ups the ante for low-impact spatial computing.

Powerful Computing Puck adds another form of input.

Familiar Android XR interface+ Access to the vast Android ecosystem.

Can be used with Macs, Windows, and SteamOS devices.

$1,099 starting price might scare off potential customers.

Sources indicate that why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Industry observers note that the world of augmented reality (AR) and extended reality (XR) glasses is really starting to get interesting. This is particularly true of so-called “self-contained” systems that don’t rely solely on your smartphone or tablet to deliver content. The Xreal Aura, which was co-developed with Google, is the latest in the Android XR field, and it’s quite an ambitious project.

Although the Aura looks somewhat similar to previous Xreal glasses that we’ve reviewed, the AR goes a step further with a dedicated puck powered by a Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite SoC, hand/finger tracking, and the ability to interface wirelessly with accessories like keyboards and gamepads. The Aura really promises the ability to leave your smartphone at home and serve as the only computing platform you need (with some caveats).

The Aura’s design is clearly an evolution of the Xreal One Series, but with a few key differences. You’ll find the main changes up front, where you’ll now find two forward-facing, high-precision tracking cameras mounted at the corners of the frame. These cameras are used to continually track your head position, giving you the best possible experience for 6 degrees of freedom tracking for your hands and fingers.

According to recent reports, at the center of the frame, there is a fully integrated single high-resolution camera for capturing photos or video. This was previously a separate add-on module for Xreal One Series AR glasses. There’s a red LED that illuminates when you’re recording so that people around you are made well aware of what’s going on if they have objections.

Your primary focal point, however, will be looking through the lenses, which are augmented by dual Sony-manufactured micro-OLED displays. You get one micro-OLED display per eye, each offering 1920 x 1200 resolution, a 120 Hz refresh rate, and maximum brightness of 1,050 nits. However, there’s a major upgrade in the field of view (FoV), as the Aura expands to 70 degrees, up from 57 degrees on the One Pro.

Sources indicate that the Aura is available in two SKUs to support the interpupillary distance (IPD) of a wide range of people. The Medium SKU supports people with an IPD of 60 to 66 mm, while the Large SKU ranges from 66 mm to 72 mm.

Given that the Aura is the flagship of Xreal’s AR/XR glasses lineup, it comes with electrochromic dimming for the lenses, which can automatically adjust transparency levels, or you can manually make adjustments (there are five levels of transparency available).

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

According to recent reports, the arms of the Aura look nearly identical to the ones you find on members of the One Series glasses. On the bottom is a red button, which, when pressed, allows you to manually adjust the brightness levels of the Aura. Directly adjacent is a rocker that allows you to control the volume. There’s another button on the top of the right arm that, when pressed once, takes you to the home menu. Double-pressing the button brings up the capture menu for taking pictures or videos with the forward-facing camera.

Bose-tuned speakers are also built into the arms of the Aura and feature an open-ear design so that you can remain engaged with what’s happening in your environment.

USB-C, Bluetooth 5.3, Wi-Fi 6E, GPS.

Sources indicate that xreal takes a two-pronged approach to hardware with the Aura. At a base level, the Aura is powered by the X1S Spatial Coprocessor, which allows you to experience traditional AR functionality with smartphones, tablets, PCs, and Macs, as you would with previous Xreal glasses.

But the real magic happens with the Xreal Computing Puck, which is a separate device that connects to the Aura using a USB-C cable. The puck looks and feels like a slightly oversized smartphone, albeit without a display. In place of the display, you’ll find a large touch-sensitive surface that can be used to interface with the Android XR interface.

Industry observers note that the puck is powered by Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon Reality Elite Platform, which delivers 48 TOPS of AI computing power. It comes in 12GB RAM/256GB storage or 16GB RAM/512GB SKUs — our review unit was spec’d with the former. The puck features a 4,455 mAh battery that powers the glasses, and it even incorporates a fingerprint reader for authentication purposes in Android XR. The puck also fully supports Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.3; the latter of which is essential for supporting Bluetooth accessories.

The puck is quite beefy, measuring roughly 5.85 x 2.85 x 0.5 inches and weighing 9.3 ounces. I had no matter just slipping the puck into my pants pocket, but Xreal also includes a detachable clip if you want to attach it to your pants pocket or other clothing. The puck also features a cooling fan to keep temperatures in check. Indeed, the device can get warm to the touch (after all, it’s basically a powerful screenless smartphone with a 4,455 mAh battery) during use – which explains why Xreal includes the clip and probably doesn’t want you putting the puck in your pocket, like I was prone to do.

It has been revealed that my Aura review unit also came with an Xreal Keyboard and an Xreal Game Controller. Both connect to the Aura using Bluetooth and were easily set up by pairing them within the Bluetooth menu under Settings.

In a recent development, the keyboard is battery-powered and is recharged using a USB-C port at the top (just above the F7 key). It’s a nifty design that neatly folds when not in use. Interestingly, I couldn’t find a way to “lock” the hinged part of the keyboard when it’s fully extended. Because of this, you can’t use the keyboard sitting on your lap with your legs spread slightly apart, as the keyboard will simply collapse and fall to the floor if you apply any kind of pressure. You’ll either need to put your legs together or place the keyboard on a desk or table, which isn’t exactly ideal if you like the more “freeing” aspect of using XR glasses.

With that noted, the keyboard is a lifesaver when it comes to text entry, be it for entering web addresses, writing emails, or anything that requires frequent use of the keyboard. It sure beats waving your fingers around to input text.

Recent findings suggest that the game controller features an Xbox-style layout with four face buttons for gaming, two thumbsticks, a D-pad, and a Google Gemini/Home button. There are two shoulder buttons at the top and two triggers (with modes to function as microswitch triggers or Hall Effect analog triggers). There are also two remappable macro buttons under the shoulder buttons and two additional macro buttons on the underside of the controller (which can be turned off with physical switches).

In a recent development, not only does the controller feature built-in rumble, but it also incorporates a 6-axis gyroscope for aiming and finger controls and a 3.5mm headphone jack built into the bottom of the unit. But perhaps the most interesting feature is a magnetic faceplate that breaks into three pieces. The main piece covers the face buttons, D-pad, and thumbsticks. The other two pieces cover the hand grips. You can purchase separate pieces to customize the look of the controller if you wish.

Sources indicate that I found the controller comfortable to use, with a nice textured plastic finish for your palms to rest on (the bottom of the controller features a similar texture, but has a rubber coating over the plastic for better grip). And although the controller is designed for Bluetooth use with the Aura, it does feature a USB-C port and a USB dongle for connecting it wirelessly to a PC.

It has been revealed that another nice touch is that Xreal includes a charging dock for the controller that plugs in with a lengthy USB-A to USB-C cable. The controller itself charges with four pogo pins mounted on top of the dock (or via USB-C if you prefer).

After removing the Aura from its retail box, I wanted to get into the action rapidly and didn’t bother initially charging the puck. I used the included USB-C to USB-C cable to plug from the left arm of the Aura into the dedicated USB-C port on the bottom of the puck. Next, I pressed the power button on the puck, after which the glasses sprang to life and began the setup process.

Industry observers note that after taking some time to get used to dragging and pinching through the Android XR interface using my fingers, the experience began to feel almost natural. I was able to pinch to open apps, have multiple apps open at once, and drag or resize windows in my viewing space on command.

Industry observers note that I was able to access all the typical stock apps like Chrome, Gmail, and Google Photos, which, of course, carried over my favorites, emails, and photos/vidoes, respectively. I spent quite a bit of time going down memory lane, watching videos of my two sons when they were toddlers among the hundreds of videos I have stored in Google Photos. It was also great to be navigating around the UI or working in the app, then seeing a notification pop up telling me that an email had arrived. I would then pinch the notification with my fingers to open Gmail.

The possibilities of how you can use the Aura are almost endless, and you can even mix other computing devices into the formula. For example, I was able to plug a USB-C cable from my MacBook Air into the second USB-C port on the puck (that’s usually reserved for recharging the puck). In an instant, my MacBook Air’s display was mirrored onto the glasses in front of me. So I could have Google Docs open as I typed, while having the Android XR native Gmail and YouTube apps flanking the virtual MacBook Air display.

It has been revealed that it’s a similar experience with handheld gaming consoles. I was successfully able to connect a Lenovo Legion Go S (SteamOS) and an MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ (Windows 11) to the Aura glasses without problem, enjoying a vast library of games in fully immersive glory.

Sources indicate that the native gaming experience isn’t bad either; I loaded up games like Fortnite and spent an hour toiling around in Grand Theft Auto III for a nostalgic treat ahead of the release of Grand Theft Auto VI. The Xreal Game Controller made playing these games a breeze.

But I also used the Aura glasses for more mundane tasks. I was able to walk around the house, performing my usual chores, with a shrunken YouTube window playing videos in the top right corner of my field of view. True multitasking is at hand, folks.

I should note that open-air speakers sounded good, but not great. They sounded similar to the Bose-tuned speakers in the older Xreal One Pro. There's a good level of bass, and overall clarity is good. However, if you want a more immersive audio experience, the design of the Aura allows you to easily throw on a pair of headphones or wireless earbuds to compensate for any audio shortcomings.

It has been revealed that the Xrea Aura is a true workhorse when it comes to spatial computing. By putting the bulk of the computing hardware into a smartphone-shaped Computing Puck, you have a low-impact way of experiencing XR without the hassle of wearing a bulky headset.

You can navigate the user interface using your hands, or the touch service of the puck. And for more specialized tasks, Xreal offers its own-branded keyboard and gamepad accessories (although you are free to use your own Bluetooth-enabled accessories).

Not only do you have access to the vast Android app ecosystem, but you can also connect to devices running Windows, macOS, or even SteamOS.

According to recent reports, there’s a lot going on with this device, and there are limitless possibilities for how you could use the Aura. The only problem is that most people don’t have limitless funds, so the $1,099 price tag of our review unit (12GB RAM, 256GB of storage) is sure to give many people pause. Stepping up to 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage takes the price to $1,299. If you add in the Xreal Keyboard and Xreal Game Controller, the total cost of our review unit comes in at $1,277 ($1,477 for the 16GB/512GB configuration).

That’s a lot to ask for what is essentially a niche device. However, if you want a truly immersive XR experience that is not weighed down by geeky-looking headsets, it’s hard to argue with what Xreal is offering with the Aura.

When he is not consuming copious amounts of tech news, he can be found enjoying the NC mountains or the beach with his wife and two sons.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Industry observers note that ask one of the newest language models whether a backpack comes in green, and it'll usually admit it doesn't know. Ask it how to return that backpack, and it may send the customer to a returns page, an account screen, and a return label that the store has never had. That's still a hallucination: an answer that sounds right, comes with total confidence, and isn't true.

Whatever you're building, the fix is the same: stop trusting the model with the parts it can get wrong, and check its work before anyone sees it.

In this tutorial we'll build a small support bot for a made-up outdoor gear store, three times over. The first version is the prompt plenty of bots start with. Then we'll apply five fixes, run six tricky customer emails through every version, and finish with a bot where the model can't slip a made-up price, date, or product past the code.

An LLM hallucination is output that's fluent and confident but not backed by the facts: a product that doesn't exist, a policy nobody wrote, a date that's a week out, or a citation to a paper that was never published. The word covers two different failures:.

Each one needs a different fix, so it helps to keep them apart.

It has been revealed that A language model writes by predicting likely text, one token at a time. It has no separate store of facts it checks against, and nothing in that process says "stop, you don't know this". Training adds to the problem. OpenAI's research on why language models hallucinate points out that when models are graded only on how many answers they get right, a guess scores better than "I don't know", so they learn to guess.

A few things make it worse in your app:.

Newer models are much better at the first one. They'll often say they don't know a price rather than invent one. But they still fill gaps with what's typical, and what's typical isn't always what's true for your business. You can't train that out of a model you call through an API. What you can change is what you ask it to do, what you give it, and what you check.

According to recent reports, A made-up answer costs more than one bad reply. Some of the costs are already on the record:.

In a support inbox, the cost is quieter but adds up: a refund you didn't owe, or a customer who goes looking for a live chat button that isn't there and doesn't come back.

Northwind Outdoor sells four things: two packs, a rain cover, and a tent. It has two orders on file and three short policies. Here's all of it:.

Six emails come in, and each one is there to trip the bot in a different way:.

Industry observers note that the traps: the 40L pack doesn't come in green, but the 28L does. The 40L is water-resistant, not waterproof. There's no 60L. Whether the return is allowed depends on a membership, a sale price, and a count of days since delivery. The tracking details are in one order record. And the store has no price match policy at all.

Make a folder, add "type": "module" to its package.json, and install the Anthropic SDK and Zod:.

Every version calls the model through one small helper:.

Recent findings suggest that we're using Claude Opus 5.5 at low effort. These are short, simple replies, so the model doesn't need to think for long. Swap in any model you like, because none of the fixes depend on it.

It has been revealed that opus 5.5 didn't invent a single price, colour, or delivery date across the six emails. Every reply mentioned it couldn't see the store's details. That's real progress compared with older models, but look at what it said instead. Here's the reply to the email about a pack the store doesn't sell:.

It treats the Ridgeline 60L as real and offers to help pick a fit. The other replies made up the store around the customer:.

Northwind has none of those. None of it is a wild guess: it's what a typical online store has. That's exactly why it's dangerous. A customer who goes looking for the live chat or the newsletter discount won't find it, and the bot never answered the question anyway.

It has been revealed that the model can't know Northwind's prices, so give them to it. This is the idea behind retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): find the records that matter and put them in the prompt. Our store is small enough to send all of it.

Two things changed. The store data goes in the system prompt, wrapped in tags so the model can tell data from instructions. And the prompt tells it to answer only from that data. Here's the green pack email again:.

Right on all three counts, and it even pointed to the pack that does come in green. The return, which needs four facts from two places, came back right as well:.

It has been revealed that delivered October 6, a Trail Club member, so 60 days, so December 5. Bought on sale, so store credit for what was paid, not the list price. Version 2 got all six emails right.

The last line of that prompt matters as much as the data: "If the answer isn't in the data, say you don't know and that a team member will reply by email." Without it, a model that can't find the answer has to choose between letting the customer down and guessing, and training has taught it to guess. With it, "I don't know" is a right answer, not a failure.

The price match email is the test, since the store data indicates nothing about price matching:.

It noted it didn't know, passed the question to a person, and answered the parts it could from the data.

If version 2 got everything right, why build a version 3? Because "right on this run" isn't the same as "right every time":.

The next three fixes take the facts and the rules away from the model completely.

Industry observers note that version 3 splits the work into three steps. First, the model reads the email, but instead of writing a reply, it fills in a form. Every field is a choice from a list, a yes or no, or text copied from the email:.

In a recent development, zod describes the form, and z.toJSONSchema() turns it into a JSON schema for the API's structured outputs. The API holds the model to that schema, so product can only be one of our four product IDs, not_sold, or none. There's no way for it to answer ridgeline-60. Zod then checks the answer again, so the rest of the code gets a typed object. SitePoint's guide to LLM structured output with JSON Schema goes deeper on this pattern.

Here's what it read from the 60L email:.

The model is still reading natural language, which it's very good at. It just isn't trusted to know what the store sells anymore.

Recent findings suggest that A form also makes the model's mistakes easy to see. The first time I ran this, the form had no asks_something_else field, and the model filed the price match email under product. The reply didn't make anything up, but the email never reached a person. In version 2, a mistake like that would be hidden inside a paragraph. Here it was one wrong value in a JSON object, and the fix was one more field.

In a recent development, if all you need from this step is decisions like these, a model built for typed answers can do it faster and for less. Our typed AI pipeline tutorial builds the same kind of email sorter with Jev and Clairic.

Second step: plain code takes the form, looks up the product and the order, applies the rules, and does the maths. What comes out is a list of facts in plain sentences:.

For the return email, that gives:.

It has been revealed that every number in there was worked out by code that does the same thing every time, and that you can unit test. The 34 days, the December 5 deadline, and the $151.20 in store credit come out the same on every run, whatever the model does.

The last rule in decide() matters most. If an email asks something the rules don't cover, the facts say so and the email goes to a person. Code decides when to say "I don't know", not the model.

According to recent reports, third step: the model writes the reply from the facts and nothing else. Writing is the one job here it does better than code.

Even with the right facts, a model writing a reply can still add something: a helpful "ships in 1–2 business days", or a price it remembers from somewhere. So the last step checks the reply. Anything that looks like a number, an order number, or a product name has to appear in the email or the facts:.

It's simple on purpose. It doesn't understand the reply. It just refuses to let through a value that came from nowhere, and that covers the hallucinations that cost money: prices, dates, quantities, and products. Nothing in the reply can talk it out of a result.

The writer runs the check on every draft:.

If a draft fails, the model gets one retry and is told exactly which values weren't in the facts. If the retry fails too, the customer gets the facts as a plain list. That's less charming, but it's true.

It has been revealed that A check like this will raise false alarms, and that's fine. On my first run, it read a line about the tent's 2.1 kg weight as a product called "Weighs 2" and sent the draft back for a retry. The weight was right, and it was the only thing flagged. A false alarm costs a few seconds. A missed one costs a customer. I tightened the patterns (the version above has the fix), but I'd still rather it flag too much than too little.

It has been revealed that it's the same thing that separates the better agentic AI coding tools from autocomplete: they run the tests and read the errors instead of trusting their first draft. Model output isn't finished until something other than the model has checked it.

Sources indicate that this script sends each email through all three versions, saves every reply, and runs the check from Fix 5 over all of them. Versions 1 and 2 are checked against everything the store knows:.

Industry observers note that the check caught one thing in version 1: the "1–2 business days" it made up for processing an order. It missed the "up to 24 hours" for tracking in the same reply, but only because $24 is the rain cover's price, so 24 counted as a known number. And it couldn't catch the invented returns page or live chat at all, because they aren't numbers. That's why the check is the last fix, not the only one.

Reading all 18 replies, here's how each version did:.

Version 3 was less helpful than version 2 in one place. It couldn't give the rain cover's price, because decide() only adds facts about the product the email names. Version 2 had the whole store to look at. In version 3, the fix is a rule you write once: when a product has an add-on, include the add-on's facts too.

Here's version 3's reply to the price match email:.

No model is free of hallucinations, so you can't stop one from ever making something up. What you can do is build so a made-up detail can't reach a customer: let code own the facts, and check the model's output against them before it's used. Where it matters, send anything your rules don't cover to a person.

Industry observers note that it cuts them a lot, because the model no longer has to guess facts it was never given. In our test, putting the store's data in the prompt took the bot from no useful answers to six right ones. It doesn't stop the model misreading what it retrieved, mixing up two records, or filling a gap the retrieved text leaves. Pair it with a way out and a check on the output.

Not really. Temperature controls how random the wording is. A low temperature makes the model give the same answer more often, including the same wrong answer.

Recent findings suggest that collect inputs that have tripped your app (or are likely to), write down the right answer for each, and run every version of your prompt or pipeline over the same set. Automated checks like the one in this tutorial catch made-up values. Read the replies yourself for the rest, because the made-up returns page above would pass any number check.

Sources indicate that hallucinations come from asking a model to do jobs it isn't built for: knowing facts it was never given, and running small programs in its head. The five fixes take those jobs away:.

Recent findings suggest that the model still does what it's best at: reading messy text and writing a friendly reply. It just isn't trusted with the facts anymore. From here, try a seventh email that asks two things at once, add the add-on rule to decide(), or extend the check to catch colours and sizes as well as numbers.

  • Recent findings suggest that “We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” Reps.
  • Yuang was an executive at Megaspeed, a firm that was a customer of Nvidia during Mr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China Select Committees on December 1, with an Nvidia lawyer following him on December 2, it's been confirmed. CNBC reports that the leaders of those panels broke the news today after days of speculation. Huang was asked to appear via a letter issued on November 9, just 24 hours after he admitted the affair with Alice Huang, a woman who has been accused of being a Chinese spy. Days later, it was also suggested that Mr. Huang could be issued a subpoena if he did not respond by tomorrow, November 18. That subpoena will no longer be required.

Recent findings suggest that “We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” Reps. Brian Mast, R-Fla., John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and Rick Crawford, R-Ark., the chairs of the Foreign Affairs, China Select, and Intelligence Committees, reportedly said after the news of the pair's December appearances was confirmed. "The American people need answers," they went on, noting that it would be "dangerous" to allow Chinese state actors access to advanced AI chips, the likes of which are built by Nvidia.

According to recent reports, ms. Yuang was an executive at Megaspeed, a firm that was a customer of Nvidia during Mr. Huang's tenure as CEO. Megaspeed was later added to Nvidia's no-sell list following concerns that it was involved in the smuggling of AI chips to China against U.S. export laws. Speedmatrix, a Megaspeed subsidiary, has been accused of importing Nvidia chips and then re-exporting them to China. A criminal investigation has since been launched into Megaspeed in an attempt to get to the bottom of the complicated web of AI companies and chip shipments.

Jensen Huang resigned from his role as CEO of Nvidia following his admission of an affair with Ms. Huang. Since then, reports of at least one other affair with an Nvidia employee have surfaced. Despite that fact, calls for Huang's return to the top job at Nvidia continue to gain momentum.

#34709. Industry News: AI safety legislation has a conflict-of-interest problem — Substantial US labs are warning of risk just as cheaper Chinese open-weight models erode their commercial edge

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1538 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: AI safety legislation has a conflict-of-interest problem — Substantial US labs are warning of risk just as cheaper Chinese open-weight models erode their commercial edge

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1538 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The battle for AI models and export controls continues amidst a Jensen Huang-free Nvidia.
  • Sources indicate that first off, let's take OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra.
  • But just because it was better behaved on the surface didn’t mean it was entirely safe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The battle for AI models and export controls continues amidst a Jensen Huang-free Nvidia. But who controls the flow of chips also controls the flow of leading frontier AI models. OpenAI reportedly now supports a bipartisan push in the U.S. Congress to restrict China's access to advanced AI accelerators and equipment. But are the additional AI safety concerns genuine, or are they also a convenient way to shore up its position at the top of a fast-moving industry? We speak to experts like Max von Thun, director of Open Markets Institute Europe, to find out more.

Sources indicate that first off, let's take OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra. The organization launched the model in September with eye-popping claims that it was the firm’s most capable and best-aligned system yet. OpenAI’s own testing suggested that Astra was much better at following instructions and respecting boundaries. In one internal computer-use safety benchmark, the proportion of misaligned outcomes fell from 18.8% with GPT-5.6 Sol to 3.4% with Astra.

But just because it was better behaved on the surface didn’t mean it was entirely safe. OpenAI noted Astra’s written reasoning was harder to monitor than its predecessor’s when they were testing its ability to evade oversight. The model began to recognize when it was being watched and altered its explanations to suit the study, making it harder to tell when it was actually doing something they didn’t want.

It’s a classic problem for AI alignment experts to try and resolve.

It has been revealed that for years, developers have relied on monitoring an AI model's chain of thought — its written working — to understand what it is doing. But if increasingly powerful AI models become better at hiding their reasoning processes, that oversight becomes harder to do.

OpenAI indicates that Astra still struggles to hide reasoning when it’s carrying out complex tasks, and its evaluation results suggest it has strong overall alignment, but there are worrying signs of a trade-off here.

Those worrying signs become even more so when AI systems are being deployed with more autonomy. In July, OpenAI models ducked its internal evaluation restrictions to gain access to research infrastructure and compromised systems belonging to Hugging Face, and to IT systems controlled by the Australian and Canadian governments.

Industry observers note that against that backdrop, calls for stronger safety measures seem entirely reasonable. But Max von Thun, director of Open Markets Institute Europe, believes the debate risks overlooking an uncomfortable conflict of interest. "I think a lot of these views about AI safety are very genuinely held," he told Tom’s Hardware Premium in an interview.

But commercial considerations loom large, he reckons. Companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are spending huge sums developing and deploying models, while facing questions about whether their competitive advantages can survive the arrival of increasingly capable, cheaper alternatives — particularly as they go out and seek funding from the public through an IPO. "They don't have huge moats, even if they’ve acquired a lot of users,” von Thun said. “They’re definitely vulnerable.”.

In a recent development, those vulnerabilities are becoming increasingly obvious. A September report from Mozilla estimated the capability gap between leading closed American models and their open-weight competitors had narrowed to just over four months.

That matters because open-weight models give people the freedom not to rely on a organization’s subscription services. They can be deployed on infrastructure controlled by the customer, modified for specialised tasks, and operated at lower costs. But to the discomfort of U.S. companies, many of them are based in China. And it’s at that point that AI safety gets muddled with geopolitics.

Recent findings suggest that in July, Axios reported that OpenAI and Anthropic, despite their fierce commercial rivalry, had found a common cause: warning U.S. policymakers about the dangers of powerful Chinese open-weight models. Kristy Loke, an AI governance researcher at King's College London who specialises in China's approach to the technology, questions the timing. "It's very suspicious timing asking for pacing," she told Tom's Hardware Premium, referring to calls for slowing frontier AI development just as Chinese open-weight models are undercutting their American rivals on price.

Industry observers note that loke believes companies genuinely worry about the risks. But she also thinks they're worried about their commercial prospects. "they're calling for pacing because they have some safety concerns, they have some commercial anxiety," she said.

She believes some influential people in American AI have increasingly sought to "paint open models in a very bad light", portraying them as inherently less secure than closed alternatives. Yet the risks of AI systems misbehaving aren't restricted to models developed in China, as OpenAI's own incidents demonstrate.

But open-weight models come with their own risks. Because their underlying parameters can be modified, third parties can create and distribute "abliterated" models, removing the refusal behaviours designed to prevent AI from responding to potentially harmful requests. Many of these models are available on platforms including Hugging Face. “They’re not adding in new behaviour; they’re just removing this refusal behaviour,” stated Catherine Flick, professor of ethics and games technology at the University of Staffordshire, in an interview with Tom’s Hardware Premium. Abliterating models doesn’t make them more capable, Flick said, but it does mean they can answer questions they previously wouldn’t have been willing to. That also means those responses might not have been tested for accuracy or hallucinations.

Sources indicate that those in favour of open-weight models like DeepSeek and Qwen say that removing those guardrails helps security researchers understand how AI behaves. Flick said that’s plausible, but “I just don’t really buy it,” she said. She reckons that the negative potential outputs outweigh the positive case for abliteration because when they’re publicly available, preventing their misuse becomes tricky. American labs clearly have commercial reasons to criticise open-weight competitors because the latter undercuts their economics, but it also doesn’t mean their concerns about safety aren’t valid, too.

Sources indicate that von Thun fears that could result in precisely the wrong kind of regulation. "I think what we should not be doing is allowing the companies to basically form a safety cartel," he remarked.

Yet U.S. AI companies benefit from the government's determination to maintain its advantage over China. Von Thun argues the Trump administration has created an environment in which economic power translates into political influence, allowing major technology companies to invoke national security concerns when arguing for policies that may also serve their commercial interests. But that could backfire. "I think completely closing off the market to AI products from other countries, including China, would not be the right approach," von Thun said.

Part of the reason that wouldn’t be the right approach is that the idea that the United States is focused on developing AI responsibly while China isn’t is a fallacy. Just earlier this month, Reuters reported that ByteDance had established a dedicated Alignment & Preparedness team, recruiting researchers to investigate safety risks arising from increasingly capable AI systems.

It has been revealed that for von Thun, the solution is to prevent either industry or geopolitical competition from determining what safety means. He points to the European Union's AI Act, which establishes obligations for developers of general-purpose AI models classified as posing systemic risks. The obligations require companies to conduct model evaluations, adversarial testing, cybersecurity measures and also to report serious incidents.

Industry observers note that the opposition to the EU’s AI Act from American tech companies, U.S. politicians and the general public who grouse about the way it delays access to cutting-edge models for Europe’s 450 million citizens demonstrates that these provisions don't automatically solve the alignment problem. But they at least involve more people in the conversation about what is and isn’t acceptable for AI than just the industry's biggest participants.

Even when AI companies agree to independent oversight, they still want some say over how it works — and their own internal decision-making on what is and isn’t safe differs from that of those outside the manufacturer. Loke warns that leading AI companies are experimenting with recursive self-improvement, where models help develop their successors, potentially making it more difficult for humans to understand how decisions are being made. "They’re still attempting more risky methods to train AI that will make the AI harder to control," she remarked.

Von Thun also believes competition rules and interoperability requirements could help prevent AI companies from locking customers into proprietary ecosystems as their agents become increasingly embedded in everyday workflows.

In a recent development, there are plenty of good reasons to be concerned about alignment, particularly when the models being developed are becoming more capable and more difficult to monitor. But letting the companies responsible for building them determine what constitutes an acceptable risk, and who can compete, brings its own dangers. “I’m not saying we don’t need to worry about safety,” mentioned von Thun, “but we should about letting the companies do it.".

Sources indicate that chris Stokel-Walker is a Tom's Hardware contributor who focuses on the tech sector and its impact on our daily lives— online and offline. He is the author of How AI Ate the World, published in 2024, as well as TikTok Boom, YouTubers, and The History of the Internet in Byte-Sized Chunks.

According to recent reports, jensen Huang, the former CEO of Nvidia who resigned last week amid the fallout from two extramarital affairs, said in his first public statement since abdicating his position that he would be willing to return to the corner office at the company he co-founded."Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a statement posted on X. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.".

According to recent reports, over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me. I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA. I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO. Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours. JensenNovember 17, 2026.

Sources indicate that huang has seen public support from other tech founders and CEOs, such as SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick. They and some investors and Nvidia employees signed an online petition and have continued to be vocal on social media, namely Musk's X. President Donald Trump also said that he "would not mind" Huang's return.Huang resigned on Thursday following two scandals: one affair with Alice Huang, a former executive of Megaspeed believed by some US Intelligence officials to be a potential Chinese government asset; and another with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care and Huang's direct report.Despite Huang's apparent willingness to return, Nvidia's board doesn't seem likely to make that move. Reports yesterday claim that the board is more focused on its ongoing investigation into Huang's affairs and a national security inquiry and is not considering Huang's return. The board has also put together its own National Security and Export Control Oversight to provide high-level oversight of Nvidia’s “national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risk management,” with its National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team reporting directly to the group and to interim CEO Colette Kress.In his post on X, Huang further apologized, writing that "I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Sources indicate that type “a lighthouse on a cliff at dusk, oil painting, warm light” into a text box, wait ten seconds, and a picture that never existed appears.
  • This guide explains how text-to-image generators turn words into pixels, why they fail in predictable ways, and how to write prompts that work with the model instead of against it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Sources indicate that type “a lighthouse on a cliff at dusk, oil painting, warm light” into a text box, wait ten seconds, and a picture that never existed appears. It feels like magic, but it is a well-understood pipeline of language models, neural networks and a great deal of math. Knowing how that pipeline works makes you a better prompter, helps you diagnose bad results, and makes it easier to choose the right tool for a job.

This guide explains how text-to-image generators turn words into pixels, why they fail in predictable ways, and how to write prompts that work with the model instead of against it. It then compares five tools that consistently produce good results, starting with Pollo AI, and finishes with a practical workflow, a troubleshooting table and an FAQ. Prepares, credits and model versions change often, so confirm current details on each vendor’s site before you commit to a subscription.

Early image generators were mostly GANs, or generative adversarial networks. A GAN pits two networks against each other: a generator that produces images and a discriminator that tries to spot fakes. GANs could produce sharp faces and textures, but they were hard to train, often collapsed into repeating the same few outputs, and were poor at following free-form text.

According to recent reports, A second line of research used autoregressive models, which generate an image piece by piece the way a language model generates words. These handled text prompts better but were slow at high resolution.

In a recent development, the shift came with diffusion models. Researchers highlighted that a network trained to reverse a gradual noising process could generate images with excellent quality and diversity, and that it was far more stable to train than a GAN. Combine that with text conditioning and a compressed image representation, and you get the systems behind most of today’s tools. Newer models increasingly swap the traditional convolutional network for transformers, but the core idea of iterative denoising is still the foundation.

It has been revealed that under the hood, mainstream generators combine three ideas: a way to understand text, a way to represent images compactly, and a way to generate them gradually. The sections below follow a prompt from keystroke to finished picture.

Neural networks cannot read words, so your prompt is first split into tokens, small chunks of text such as whole words or word fragments. A text encoder then converts those tokens into an embedding, a grid of numbers that captures meaning and context. Many systems use encoders trained jointly on images and their captions, so that the text “a red bicycle” and pictures of red bicycles end up close together in the same mathematical space. Some newer systems add a large language model to understand longer, more detailed instructions.

Sources indicate that this is why wording matters. The encoder only sees what you wrote, and it has a limited capacity. A short, specific prompt produces a clear signal. A long, rambling one dilutes each instruction.

Instead of drawing on a blank canvas, the model begins with random static. The pattern of that static is controlled by a seed number. The same prompt with a different seed gives a different image, because it starts from different noise. If a tool lets you fix the seed, you can make results repeatable and change just one variable at a time.

Recent findings suggest that during training, engineers take millions of real images and add noise to them in small steps until only static remains. The network is then trained to predict the noise that was added at each step, which teaches it to reverse the process. At generation time, the model applies that skill to pure noise, removing a little at each step. Because it has learned what real images look like, the “noise” it removes gradually reveals something that looks plausible.

It has been revealed that your text embedding is fed into the network through a mechanism called cross-attention. At each step, parts of the evolving image can “look at” relevant parts of the prompt and adjust accordingly. A region that will become a lighthouse attends to the word “lighthouse”. A region that will become the sky attends to “dusk”.

A setting called classifier-free guidance, often shown as guidance scale or prompt strength, controls how strongly each step is pulled toward the prompt. The model computes one prediction with the prompt and one without it, then exaggerates the difference. A low value gives the model freedom and often more natural, varied results. A high value follows the words more literally but can produce oversaturated, over-sharpened or distorted images.

It has been revealed that running diffusion directly on full-resolution pixels would be very expensive. The idea behind Stable Diffusion, known as latent diffusion, is to compress images into a much smaller latent representation using an autoencoder. Denoising happens in that compact space, and a decoder turns the final latent back into a full image. This is a major reason high-quality generation now runs in seconds on a cloud GPU instead of minutes.

Recent findings suggest that the number of denoising steps and the scheduler, which decides how much noise to remove at each step, shape the speed and look of the result. More steps usually add detail up to a point, then give diminishing returns. Many tools hide these settings, but the trade-off is always the same: fewer steps are faster and cheaper, more steps can look more refined.

Most pipelines finish with an upscaler or refinement pass that sharpens detail and fixes small artifacts. Many tools also offer inpainting, which regenerates only a selected region, outpainting, which extends the canvas, and variations, which restart from a related image.

Industry observers note that A generator can only produce what it has learned to represent. Models are trained on very large collections of images paired with captions, and the quality, diversity and licensing of that data affect both the output and the legal picture. Models trained on more photographs tend to produce convincing photorealism. Models tuned on illustration and concept art lean toward painterly looks.

This also explains a few behaviors. Common subjects look great because the model has seen thousands of examples. Rare or very specific subjects, such as an unusual machine part or a niche cultural item, often look generic or wrong. Biases in the data can show up as stereotypes, for example in how “a doctor” or “a CEO” is depicted, so it helps to describe the people and setting you actually want.

Understanding the process explains the familiar failures:.

Pollo AI’s text to image AI is a browser-based generator built around a simple loop: write a prompt, pick a style, generate, and download. Its page highlights HD output and a wide range of looks, from photorealistic scenes to cute cartoons, anime, pencil sketches, isometric art, abstract compositions and surreal visuals. Files can be downloaded as WebP, PNG or JPEG, a practical spread for web work: WebP keeps pages light, PNG preserves clean edges and transparency-friendly graphics, and JPEG works almost everywhere.

Pollo is also part of a wider platform that covers AI video, so a still image you like can become the starting point for motion without switching ecosystems. That matters for teams producing social content, because one workflow can cover both the image and the short clip built from it.

Industry observers note that things to check: the page does not list specific model names or credit amounts, so review the current plan details before relying on it for high-volume work. Commercial use requires a paid plan.

Best for: quick, versatile image generation across many styles, especially if you also initiative to make video.

Sources indicate that midjourney has built its reputation on strong aesthetics. Images tend to arrive with polished composition, dramatic lighting and a distinctive painterly feel, which is why it is popular for concept art, mood boards, album-style visuals and editorial illustration. It offers style references and personalization, so you can steer results toward a consistent look across a project. It also supports editing and variation tools for refining a chosen image.

The trade-offs are practical. It is a paid service, and its prompts reward experimentation over literal instruction following, so you sometimes get something beautiful that is not exactly what you described.

Best for: artistic, high-impact visuals where mood matters more than exact specification.

It has been revealed that adobe Firefly focuses on professional workflows and commercial confidence. Adobe describes Firefly’s own models as trained on licensed content such as Adobe Stock and public-domain material, and it attaches Content Credentials metadata that records AI involvement. It connects with tools many teams already use, including Photoshop features like generative fill and generative expand, which suits designers who edit as much as they generate.

Firefly also provides controls such as style and composition references. Its results can feel cleaner and more commercial than Midjourney’s, which is an advantage for marketing assets and a limitation if you want a wild artistic look.

Best for: marketing and design teams that need editing tools and clearer licensing.

It has been revealed that ideogram is known for rendering legible text inside images, a task where many generators struggle. That makes it a strong choice for posters, social graphics, logo concepts, packaging mockups and product visuals that need a headline or short phrase to read correctly. It also offers style controls and a community gallery that doubles as a prompt library.

Industry observers note that even so, long paragraphs of on-image text can still go wrong. Keep the copy to a few words, put it in quotation marks in the prompt, and describe the lettering style.

Best for: graphics that combine imagery with short, readable text.

Leonardo AI is built for creators who want more control. It offers multiple models, fine-tuning options, image-to-image guidance and a canvas for editing, with a particular following among game artists and designers who need consistent characters and assets. Features such as reference-based generation help keep a character recognizable across many scenes.

The wide set of options is powerful but means a steeper learning curve than a one-box generator, and credit systems can take time to understand.

Best for: consistent characters, game and concept assets, and consumers who like tuning settings.

A reliable prompt has five parts. Put the most important part first, because it often carries the most weight.

Compare weak prompts with stronger ones:.

Sources indicate that how do text-to-image generators work? They convert your prompt into a numerical representation, then use a diffusion model to remove noise from a random starting image step by step, guided by that representation, until a matching picture appears.

According to recent reports, which text-to-image tool is best? It depends on the job. Pollo AI suits fast, varied generation, Midjourney suits artistic work, Adobe Firefly suits commercial design, Ideogram suits images with text and Leonardo AI suits tuned, consistent assets.

Why does the same prompt give different results? Each run starts from a different random seed. Fixing the seed, where a tool allows it, makes results more repeatable.

Can I use AI-generated images commercially? Often yes, but the rules differ by tool and plan. Pollo, for example, notes that commercial use requires a paid plan. Always check the current terms.

How do I get readable text in an AI image? Use a tool strong at text, keep the wording to a few words, and add the text in a design editor if accuracy is critical.

What file format should I download? WebP for lightweight web pages, PNG for graphics and sharp edges, JPEG for broad compatibility.

Can I turn a generated image into a video? Many platforms support it. Pollo AI, for example, also covers AI video, so you can move from a still to motion in one place.

According to recent reports, text-to-image generators work by turning language into numbers and using those numbers to guide a model that denoises random static into a picture. Once you understand that, prompts stop being guesswork: you give the model a clear subject, style and lighting, you iterate one change at a time, and you fix small flaws locally. Start with a versatile option such as Pollo AI, then add Midjourney, Firefly, Ideogram or Leonardo when a project needs their particular strengths.
